T0.p: A general heading for motifs about love, including love's effects, omens, and the art of love.

T1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 36; Halm Aesop No. 148.
T1.p: Zeus gives humans modesty, but when love comes into the world, modesty leaves.

T2.r: Krappe Science of Folklore 6f.; Penzer VII 227; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 367 n. 1; India: Thompson-Balys.
T2.p: A debate over whether men or women take greater pleasure in sex. A man who was transformed into a woman says women do, and the goddess blinds him as punishment.

T3.p: Signs or omens that predict how a love affair will turn out.

T3.1.p: A person born under the color blue is lucky in love matters.

T4.p: A person wants to learn the art of love, meaning how to win and keep a lover.

T4.1.p: A herdsman wants to learn the art of love so that he can become a holy man.

T6.p: Love is used to lure people into worshipping idols or false gods.

T8.p: Sexual desire is seen as the original sin.

T10.p: A general heading for motifs in which someone falls in love.

T10.1.p: A lazy prince is reformed and changes his ways after falling in love.

T10.1.1.p: A gambler is reformed and gives up gambling after falling in love.

T10.1.2.p: A rough, crude man is transformed into a refined, courtly gentleman because he falls in love. Love civilizes him and polishes his manners.

T10.2.p: An angel or supernatural being causes a man to fall in love against his will or without his choosing.

T10.3.p: A girl keeps falling in love again and again, becoming infatuated with one man after another.

T11.p: A person falls in love with someone they have never met or seen in person.

T11.1.r: *Type 516; *Rösch FFC LXXVII 100; *Chauvin V 132 No. 112; *Penzer X 214 s.v. “Love by mere mention”; Malone PMLA XLIII 399; *Dickson 188 n. 63; Hibbard 208 n. 18, 226 n. 1; *Cross MPh XII 612 n. 3; Moore PMLA XXIX (1914) 527f.; Fb “hår” IV 241b. — Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 7, *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T11.1.p: A person falls in love simply from hearing someone mentioned or having them described.

T11.1.1.p: Reports of a woman's beauty reach a king, and he sets out to seek her as his bride.

T11.2.r: *Types 403, 516, 900; *BP I 45ff., 443ff.; *Rösch FFC LXXVII 98; Philippson FFC L 11f.; *Penzer X 214 s.v. “love with a painting”, 263 s.v. “picture, falling in love”; Fb “portræt” II 863; *Köhler-Bolte I 127, 520ff., 527; Wesselski Archiv Orientální II 430; Herbert III 204; Oesterley No. 62.—English: Wells 81 (Sir Tristrem); Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “portrait”; Missouri French: Carrière; Arabian: Burton Nights S II 194ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham, Eberhard FFC CXX 61f., 252; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 218.
T11.2.p: A person falls in love after seeing a painting or picture of someone.

T11.2.0.1.p: A girl refuses a suitor because his picture is ugly.

T11.2.1.r: *Type 516; *Rösch FFC LXXVII 99; Köhler-Bolte I 520 ff., 527; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
T11.2.1.p: A person falls in love after seeing a statue of someone.

T11.2.1.1.r: Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 63, 76, II 476, 1090; Chinese: Chavannes 500 Contes I 374 No. 107.
T11.2.1.1.p: A young man carves a statue of a girl and then searches for a real girl who looks like the statue.

T11.3.r: *Type 516; *BP I 45; *Rösch FFC LXXVII 100; *Chauvin V 132 No. 112; *Penzer III 82 n. 2, IX 36 n. 1; *Moore PMLA XXIX 527f.; Rohde Griechische Roman 45ff.; Dunlop-Wilson II 258; Bédier Fabliaux (1895) 113ff.; *Krappe Revue Hispanique LXXXI 5ff.—Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 78, *Cross; Icelandic: M. Moe in Edda 1914 p. 245, *Boberg; Arabian: Basset 1001 Contes I 136, II 68; India: *Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 73 No. 40, 136 No. 63; Indonesia: J. Brandes Tijdschrift voor Indische Taal-, Land-, en Volkenkunde XLI 295f., 469, Jeynboll Supplement Catalogus Jav. — Madoereesche Handschriften I 53ff.; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 231; N. A. Indian (Yana): Curtin Creation Myths 425ff.; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis III 247; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 211f. No. 73, 220 No. 74.
T11.3.p: A person falls in love with someone they have seen only in a dream.

T11.3.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Persian: Carnoy 341; India: Thompson-Balys; Hindu: Penzer III 82.
T11.3.1.p: Two lovers meet and get together in their dreams.

T11.3.2.p: A person dreams of marrying someone else's wife.

T11.4.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens II 103b. nn. 169—76; India: Thompson-Balys.
T11.4.p: A person falls in love after seeing an object belonging to a princess they have never met.

T11.4.1.r: **Golther Die Jungfrau mit den goldenen Haaren (Leipzig, 1893); *Cosquin Contes indiens 50 n. 2, 351ff.; Köhler-Bolte II 328ff.; Chavannes III 258 No. 470; Icelandic: Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Philippines: Dixon 169.
T11.4.1.p: A person falls in love after seeing a hair belonging to a princess they have never met.

T11.4.1.1.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Shasta): Thompson Tales 196.
T11.4.1.1.p: A princess falls in love after seeing a hair belonging to a hero she has never met.

T11.4.2.p: A person falls in love after seeing a slipper belonging to a princess they have never met.

T11.4.3.r: Cowell Jataka IV 144; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 586.
T11.4.3.p: A person falls in love after finding a lady's wreath.

T11.4.3.1.p: A person falls in love after seeing a bouquet.

T11.4.4.p: A person falls in love after seeing the marks of a lady's teeth in a fruit she has bitten.

T11.4.5.p: A man falls in love with a lady he has never met after finding her handkerchief, which lets him feel he has seen something belonging to an unknown princess.

T11.4.6.p: A man falls in love with a woman he has never met after finding one of her ornaments, such as a ring or comb.

T11.4.7.p: A man falls in love with a girl he has never seen when he receives her amulet.

T11.5.r: Malone PMLA XLIII 400; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
T11.5.p: Someone falls in love with a reflection seen in water; in the tale the princess thus first sees the prince.

T11.5.1.r: (Narcissus.) Italian Novella: Rotunda; Ovid Metamorphoses Bk. 3.
T11.5.1.p: A person falls in love with his or her own reflection seen in water.

T11.6.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 9, V No. 9.
T11.6.p: A man wishes for a wife who is as red as blood, as white as snow, and as black as a raven.

T11.7.p: A person falls in love with someone seen in a magic mirror.

T11.8.p: A person falls in love with someone because of a beautiful voice heard.

T12.p: A prince falls in love with a woman because of a prophecy that he shall marry the fairest woman.

T13.p: A wife falls in love with a suitor because her husband praises him.

T15.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 614, II 355, 1369.
T15.p: A person falls in love the moment they first see another.

T15.1.p: A princess is so lovely that everyone who sees her falls in love with her.

T16.p: A man falls in love with a woman he sees bathing.

T16.0.1.p: A woman falls in love with a man she sees while she is bathing.

T16.0.2.p: A woman who is bathing sees a hero and falls in love with him.

T16.1.p: A man falls in love at the sight of a woman's white arms.

T16.2.p: A man falls in love with a beautiful girl when he sees her dead body.

T21.r: Schoepperle II 587a s.v. “potion”; English: Wells 80 (Sir Tristrem).
T21.p: Two people fall in love mutually after one of them accidentally drinks a love potion.

T22.p: Two people are destined by fate to become each other's future spouse.

T22.1.p: Two lovers are destined to be united before they are even born, and fate brings them together as soon as they meet.

T22.2.r: (Cf. M312.1.) Basset 1001 Contes II 208 n. 1; Finnish-Swedish: Hackman FFC VI No. 930*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 934A*; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 202 No. 149, FFC CXXVIII 179 No. 95; Japanese: Ikeda.
T22.2.p: A woman is destined from birth to become a particular man's wife, so the match is fixed in advance by fate.

T22.3.r: Icelandic: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 450a n. 534; Italian: Basile Pentamerone, Introduction; Japanese: Ikeda.
T22.3.p: A man is destined from birth to become a particular woman's husband, so the match is fixed in advance by fate.

T22.4.p: Two lovers are born at the same time and fated to marry each other, and prophecies given to both are identical.

T24.r: *Penzer VII 139 n. 2; *Rohde Der griechische Roman 157ff.; Irish myth: Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T24.p: The physical and emotional signs that a person is in love.

T24.1.r: *Penzer II 9 n. 2, 10 n., III 68 n. 1; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “amoureux”; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; Japanese: Ikeda.
T24.1.p: A person becomes sick or weak with longing for someone they love.

T24.1.1.p: A man lusts after a certain woman, has nocturnal emissions as a result, and these bring him close to death.

T24.2.r: *Type 516; *Rösch FFC LXXVII 98; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hindu: Penzer II 10 n.; Chinese: Graham.
T24.2.p: A person faints or falls unconscious because of love.

T24.2.1.p: A person faints away from love or sexual desire.

T24.2.2.p: A person faints out of fright on hearing that the person they love is going to be killed.

T24.2.3.p: A person faints on first seeing someone of extraordinary beauty.

T24.3.r: *Chauvin VI 51 No. 217 n. 2; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Göngu-Hrólfs saga 300; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T24.3.p: A person goes mad because of love.

T24.4.p: A woman takes on her lover's deformity, such as a physical defect, while talking with him.

T24.5.p: A young man's face alternates between red and white because he is in love.

T24.6.p: A lover refuses to eat or drink because of love.

T24.7.p: A person waits twenty-two years in order to see a beautiful person.

T24.8.p: A man promises to sacrifice himself in order to marry the person he loves.

T25.p: A person is miraculously healed through the power of passionate love.

T26.p: A person's attention is so distracted by the sight of their beloved that they lose track of what they are doing.

T26.1.p: A person cuts their own finger while cooking or eating because they cannot take their eyes off the beloved sitting opposite.

T27.p: A person has unusually great success in love.

T27.1.p: Thirty young girls all fall in love with the same young man.

T27.2.p: Seventy princesses fall in love with the hero, but he loves only the youngest of them.

T27.3.p: One hundred rajahs (Indian princes) all fall in love with the same woman.

T28.p: A princess falls in love with a man who is disguised as a woman.

T29.p: A general category of stories in which people fall in love in various other ways not covered by the more specific motifs.

T29.1.p: A boy and a girl fall in love when a curtain is pulled aside and they see each other.

T30.p: A general category of stories in which lovers meet, often after separation or hardship.

T31.r: As page, or the like. Dickson 143. Cf. Folie Tristan.
T31.p: The hero meets the heroine while working as a servant in her household.

T31.1.r: *Type 314; Malone PMLA XLIII 421; Boccaccio Decameron II No. 6; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
T31.1.p: The hero meets his beloved while working as a servant for the lady's father.

T32.p: The heroine cures the hero's wounds, and so they meet and fall in love.

T32.1.p: The hero is imprisoned in the heroine's father's jail, and she helps him escape.

T33.p: A man who has been transformed into an animal is kept as a pet by the heroine, and the two come together.

T34.p: Lovers first meet at a social gathering such as a party or dance.

T34.1.p: A woman pours a drink for a man at a festival and he falls in love with her at once.

T34.2.p: Two people fall in love while playing a game together.

T34.2.1.p: Two people fall in love while playing draughts (checkers).

T35.r: (Cf. R315.1.) Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière.
T35.p: A general category of stories in which lovers arrange a secret meeting at an agreed place and time.

T35.0.1.p: A lover arrives late to the rendezvous because he is held up by a person who talks endlessly.

T35.0.2.p: A lover is put into a magic sleep and so misses his appointment with his mistress.

T35.1.r: Malone PMLA XLIII 402; Nouvelles de Sens No. 3; Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: Neuman.
T35.1.p: A fountain or well is the place where lovers arrange to meet.

T35.2.p: A pavilion or summerhouse serves as the place where lovers secretly meet.

T35.3.p: A girl makes her nurse drunk so that the nurse cannot stop her from meeting her lover.

T35.4.r: (Cf. J2166.) Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 81; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T35.4.p: Lovers miss their meeting because one of them hesitates and cannot decide what to do.

T35.5.p: A lover boldly goes to visit his beloved at her husband's or father's house, despite the risk of being caught.

T36.r: Boccaccio Decameron V No. 4; von der Hagen II *xi, 71 No. 25; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T36.p: A girl sleeps out in the garden so she can meet her lover, and is found there the next morning, after which they marry.

T37.r: Boccaccio Decameron X No. 4 (Lee 313ff.); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T37.p: A lover finds his lady lying in a tomb, apparently dead, and she later wakes up and marries him.

T37.0.1.p: A wife who appears to be poisoned by her husband revives, because a student had replaced the poison with a sleeping potion and taken her from the tomb; when she wakes, he claims her as his own.

T37.1.p: A lover, finding his beloved apparently dead in her tomb, takes poison to die with her. She then wakes, learns of his mistake, and dies by sharing his fate.

T41.p: Lovers find ways to send messages or communicate with each other while apart.

T41.1.r: Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Greek: Fox 201 (Pyramus and Thisbe); Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian (Malecite): Mechling GSCan VI No. 21, (Fox): Jones PAES I 145 (the last two tell of sexual relations through hole in a tent).
T41.1.p: Lovers communicate by speaking or passing things through a hole in a wall.

T41.2.p: Lovers communicate through a hole in the floor.

T41.3.p: A signal lets a lover know when he should come to the meeting.

T42.p: Lovers carry on a conversation, often in secret or indirectly.

T42.1.p: Lovers who have never been introduced talk to each other using sign language.

T42.2.p: Lovers talk using figurative language that outsiders cannot understand.

T45.r: *Type 900; BP I 446; *Philippson FFC L 26f.; *Fb “guldrok” I 514b, “guldhaspe” I 513b.
T45.p: A lover pays someone to gain entry into a woman's room.

T46.p: A suitor gets past a watchman by trickery in order to reach the lady he wants.

T46.1.p: A young man climbs eight fences while being watched by one hundred guards in order to reach his beautiful beloved.

T47.p: A stepmother hides the heroine away whenever a suitor comes to call.

T50.p: Courtship, the process by which a person tries to win another's love and marriage.

T50.1.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 551a nn. 228—36; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 577.
T50.1.p: A girl is closely protected so that suitors cannot approach her.

T50.1.1.r: (Cf. K1349.4.) Irish myth: Cross; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 151, 165.
T50.1.1.p: A girl is kept under close watch by her mother so that suitors cannot reach her.

T50.1.2.p: A girl is kept under close watch by her father so that suitors cannot reach her.

T50.1.3.p: A girl is kept from suitors by a witch-like old woman who guards her.

T50.1.4.p: A cat and a dog stand guard over a beautiful woman who is kept imprisoned.

T50.2.p: A king loves his daughter so much that he refuses to marry her off to anyone.

T50.2.1.p: A king will not marry his daughter to a man he considers beneath her in rank or worth.

T50.3.r: (Cf. T111.) S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 158f.
T50.3.p: A supernatural being asks for a girl's hand in marriage.

T51.r: *Schoepperle I 188 n. 3, 202; Icelandic: Half saga ok Hálfsrekka 69, *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.
T51.p: A man sends an agent or representative to woo a bride on his behalf.

T51.1.r: *Köhler-Bolte II 328ff.; Schoepperle passim; English: Wells 43 (Arthour and Merlin); Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 159; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 210.
T51.1.p: The emissary sent to woo a lady falls in love with her and wins her for himself.

T51.1.1.p: The emissary is let into the woman's room and runs off with her.

T51.2.p: A king woos a bride through his daughter and the princess's maid.

T51.3.p: A match is arranged by showing each party a picture of the other.

T51.3.1.p: Messengers search for a wife for the hero who looks like a picture they carry with them.

T52.r: *Type 890 (Christiansen Norske Eventyr 113); *Fb “brud” IV 64a; Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 130, *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman; Greek: *Grote I 157, 163; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 57; Africa (Fang): Tessman 175f.
T52.p: A bride is bought from her family rather than won by courtship.

T52.1.r: (Cf. D212, D215.) Type 652; BP II 125; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 2.
T52.1.p: A prince buys a twig or flower from a girl's mother, which turns out to be an enchanted girl.

T52.2.p: Money paid for a bride is handed to a rejected suitor instead of the bride, to settle a dispute.

T52.3.r: East Africa: Rochemonteix Quelques Contes Nubiens (Cairo, 1888) 48ff. No. 4.
T52.3.p: A bride is bought for her weight in gold.

T52.4.p: A dowry is given to the bridegroom's side when a daughter marries.

T52.4.1.p: The size of the dowry is set by custom in the bride's family.

T52.5.p: A man tries to buy a wife, but the attempt fails or is made.

T52.6.p: A wealthy girl gives a poor suitor a necklace so he can pay the bride-price her family demands, letting him win her hand.

T52.7.p: A princess is demanded in exchange for a king or ruler sparing a palace or city from destruction.

T52.8.p: A creditor, in a law court, demands the wife of an absent debtor as payment for the debt.

T52.9.p: A village is given to a bride-to-be as part of her dowry.

T53.p: Matchmakers, people who arrange marriages between others, appear in the tale.

T53.1.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 177f., 374.
T53.1.p: A prophet in disguise acts as a matchmaker, arranging a marriage while hiding his identity.

T53.2.p: Christ acts as a matchmaker, arranging a marriage.

T53.3.p: A saint acts as a matchmaker, arranging a marriage.

T53.4.p: God is busy with arranging marriages, so the matchmaking is left to others or delayed.

T53.5.p: A barber acts as a matchmaker, arranging a marriage between two people.

T54.r: (Cf. B152.2, M302.4, T22.) Chinese: Chavannes 500 Contes I 376 No. 108.
T54.p: A bride is chosen by consulting astrology, reading her horoscope to see whether she is a good match.

T55.r: Forthputting woman. *Cross MPh XII 612 n. 3; Hibbard 208 n. 18; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
T55.p: A girl takes the initiative and pursues a man she wants to marry.

T55.1.r: *Type 314; *Dickson 144 n. 146; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman; Africa (Ibo, Nigeria): Thomas 120.
T55.1.p: A princess openly declares her love for a humble hero of low rank.

T55.1.1.p: A princess openly declares her love for a courtier.

T55.2.p: A servant girl helps a prince in exchange for his promise to make her his chief wife.

T55.3.p: A noblewoman who loves a ruler gets a friend to help her win him.

T55.4.p: A little girl offers a prince marvelous objects if he promises to marry her when she grows up.

T55.4.1.p: A bride gives a gift to her husband.

T55.5.p: A princess pretends to be sick so that she can win a hero, insisting that only marriage to him will cure her.

T55.6.p: A man or woman is made to show off or display a figure, such as a body or a shape, as a way of being noticed or tested in courtship.

T55.6.1.p: Young women ask the hero to show off his figure or body, so they can admire him as a possible husband.

T55.7.p: A princess chooses her own husband from among the young men present, rather than waiting to be chosen.

T55.8.r: Krappe Revue Hispanique LXXXI (1933); Irish myth: Cross.
T55.8.p: A princess declares her love to a man by handing him a cup of drink at a feast.

T55.9.p: A girl sends a harper to carry her love message to the man she wants.

T55.10.p: A princess offers a reward to anyone who can get a prince to marry her.

T55.11.p: A princess changes her own shape or appearance in order to attract a lover.

T56.p: Ways or devices by which a person draws the attention and affection of a sweetheart.

T56.1.p: A bride is drawn toward her suitor or husband by the sound of music.

T56.1.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 209 No. 157; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: Kroeber JAFL XXI 224; West Indies: Flowers 577.
T56.1.1.p: A bride is drawn toward her suitor or husband by the sound of a flute.

T56.2.p: An image of the God of Love is sent to bring the bride to her suitor.

T56.3.p: A forgotten fiancée sends her lover a false diamond inscribed with Christ's last words, "Oh Lord why hast Thou forsaken me?" and the lover returns to her.

T56.4.p: A beautiful woman is lured or drawn in by a wonderful flower.

T57.p: A person openly states their love for another, as a way of wooing.

T57.1.p: A lover reveals his feelings by showing his beloved her own reflection, implying that she is the one he loves.

T58.p: A suitor woos a bride who is both strong and beautiful, usually by facing a difficult test or contest.

T61.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman.
T61.p: A formal promise of marriage between two people, agreed before the wedding.

T61.1.p: Two lovers seal their betrothal by each drinking the other's blood.

T61.2.p: Lovers who must part promise not to marry anyone else for seven years.

T61.3.p: At the betrothal, a maiden makes a shirt for her lover as a token of her commitment.

T61.4.p: A betrothal ceremony, the formal ritual by which a couple is promised to marry.

T61.4.1.p: The liquor or drink brewed specifically for use at a betrothal ceremony.

T61.4.2.p: At the betrothal ceremony, the bride and groom each drink from a shared loving-cup.

T61.4.3.p: In an engagement ritual, a go-between sprinkles the girl with flour.

T61.4.4.p: A token of betrothal is sent to the parents of a proposed groom; if they accept it, they agree to the proposed match.

T61.4.5.p: A couple is betrothed by the giving of a gold ring.

T61.4.5.1.p: A lover on his deathbed sends his ring to his sweetheart, as a token of their betrothal.

T61.5.p: Children born on the same night are betrothed to each other.

T61.5.1.p: A hero and a princess are betrothed while both are still infants in the cradle.

T61.5.2.p: Two children, aged ten and twelve, betroth themselves to each other.

T61.5.3.r: Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1097; Madagascar: Renel I 168ff. No. 30.
T61.5.3.p: Children not yet born are promised in marriage to each other.

T62.r: *Type 900; BP 443ff.; *Philippson FFC L 21f.; *Chauvin V 234 No. 134 n. 1; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T62.p: A princess must marry the first man who asks for her hand.

T62.1.p: A man must marry the first woman who gives him alms.

T62.2.p: A minister's daughter must marry the first unmarried man who arrives.

T63.p: A princess's husband is chosen when an elephant bows to a particular man.

T64.r: *Thien Motive 4; Chaucer’s Clerk’s Tale; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
T64.p: A king seeks a bride only because his counsellors insist, not from his own wish.

T65.p: Restrictions or conditions that govern when and how a betrothal may be made.

T65.1.p: A maiden will not pledge herself in betrothal to two brothers one after the other.

T65.1.1.p: A girl who is formally betrothed can never marry anyone else, even if the first match is prevented from happening.

T65.2.p: A mercenary soldier, or an exile, is considered unsuitable as a husband.

T66.p: A general category of stories in which someone receives help in winning the love or hand of another person.

T66.1.r: *Type 506; India: Thompson-Balys. See references for E341 (the grateful dead).
T66.1.p: A dead man whom the hero had earlier treated kindly returns the favor by helping the hero win a princess.

T66.2.p: Small boys whom the hero had earlier helped repay him by aiding him in winning a girl.

T67.p: A general category in which a prince is offered as the reward or prize for a task.

T67.1.p: A girl is promised in marriage to a prince as payment for breaking a spell that has turned him into an animal or monster.

T67.2.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone II Nos. 2, 5; India: Thompson-Balys.
T67.2.p: A girl is promised in marriage to a prince as payment for curing him of an illness or affliction.

T67.3.p: A prince promises to marry the girl who can rescue him from an embarrassing predicament.

T67.3.1.p: A king is placed under a magic spell by a doll and is rescued by a girl who frees him. In return he agrees to marry her.

T68.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 130f.; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T68.p: A general category in which a princess is offered as the reward or prize for a deed.

T68.1.r: *Types 300, 301, 302, 303, 304, 506, 653; *Hartland Perseus III 1—65; *MacCulloch Childhood 17f.; Irish myth: Cross; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 7; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 420; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 89 No. 5.
T68.1.p: A princess is promised in marriage to whoever rescues her or performs a particular feat.

T68.2.p: An earl's daughter is given as the reward to a knight who helps kill a fierce buffalo.

T68.3.p: A man who saves his country is rewarded with the hand of a princess.

T68.4.p: A defeated king gives the hero his daughter in marriage along with power over his kingdom.

T68.5.p: A girl agrees to marry a hunter if he promises to restore her monkey brothers to human form.

T69.p: A miscellaneous group of courtship motifs that do not fit the more specific headings.

T69.1.r: (Seven—seven, fifty—fifty, etc.) Type 303*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 303*; Greek: Aeschylus Prometheus Bound 853.
T69.1.p: A large number of brothers each seek a different one of a large number of sisters as a wife.

T69.1.1.p: Three brothers each marry one of three sisters.

T69.1.2.p: Seven princes each seek to marry one of seven princesses.

T69.2.r: Type 516; Rösch FFC LXXVII 101; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
T69.2.p: Parents arrange marriages for their children without the children knowing about it beforehand.

T69.2.1.p: Parents seek one of their seven daughters as a wife for their son, without the daughters or son having agreed.

T69.2.2.p: A princess's parents decide that she may marry only a man who weighs no more than she does.

T69.3.p: A man offers his daughter in marriage in exchange for being set free.

T69.3.1.p: A raja (ruler) betroths his daughter to a visitor's son as payment to make up for a killing.

T69.4.p: A shy suitor addresses his courtship to an oak tree instead of to the woman he loves.

T69.5.p: A father punishes his daughter by marrying her to a poor man.

T70.p: A general category for tales in which a lover is rejected or scorned in love.

T71.r: *Dickson 87ff. nn. 50, 55; Penzer II 109, 120ff., III 109f., IV 91, 104ff., V 259 n. 1; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
T71.p: Women who are scorned or rejected in love.

T71.1.p: A woman scorned in love dies by accident.

T71.2.p: A woman takes revenge on someone who scorned her love.

T71.2.1.p: A woman who has been scorned in love complains about the man's coldness.

T72.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
T72.p: A man wins a woman's love and then scorns her.

T72.1.p: A girl who runs away with a man who pretends to love her is made by him to strip naked.

T72.2.p: A nobleman marries a poor girl and then abandons her.

T72.2.1.p: A prince marries a disdainful girl and then punishes her.

T72.3.p: A woman sets out to kill the man who won her love and then scorned her. A ruler brings about their reconciliation.

T72.4.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 33; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T72.4.p: A woman secretly entertains two lovers on alternate nights. They discover the deception and publicly scorn her.

T75.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 357.
T75.p: A man is scorned or rejected by the woman he loves.

T75.0.1.p: Suitors are treated badly or cruelly by the woman they court.

T75.0.2.p: A mortal woman turns away a god in favor of a human lover.

T75.1.p: An unloved suitor who scorns others is punished.

T75.2.p: A scorned lover kills the rival who succeeded in winning the beloved.

T75.2.1.p: A man whose suit was rejected takes revenge by killing the rival who won the woman's love.

T75.3.r: English romance: Malory X 86; Spanish: Childers.
T75.3.p: A man expresses his unrequited love for a woman in a song or poem.

T75.4.p: A woman mocks or humiliates a man who abandoned his wife to be with her.

T75.5.p: A man rejected in love withdraws from the world and becomes a religious hermit.

T75.6.p: A scorned lover throws himself from the top of a minaret to his death, but a divine hand catches him in mid-fall.

T76.r: *Type 900; *BP I 443ff.; *Philippson FFC L 14; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 10.
T76.p: A princess insults her suitors by calling them ugly names.

T77.p: A noble maiden who is to marry a knight disguises herself as a beggar's daughter to test or annoy him.

T80.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
T80.p: A general heading for tales in which love ends in tragedy.

T81.r: *Penzer II 8, 9 n. 2, 10, V 39, VII 69 n. 1, 103, 258, VIII 98; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 69, 209 No. 157.
T81.p: A person dies because of love, either from grief, longing, or the strain of passion.

T81.1.p: A man dies at the bedside of his dying sweetheart.

T81.2.p: A person dies of love that is not returned.

T81.2.1.p: A rejected lover takes his own life.

T81.2.1.1.p: A rejected woman threatens to take her own life.

T81.3.p: A girl dies by falling dead across her lover's body.

T81.4.p: A man dies when the bride who had been denied to him kisses him.

T81.5.p: A sick lover dies from the exertion of embracing his beloved.

T81.6.p: A girl kills herself after her lover dies.

T81.7.p: A woman dies on hearing news that her lover or husband has died.

T81.8.p: A wife swallows a hot coal and dies because her husband has been unfaithful to her.

T82.r: Herbert III 212; Oesterley No. 281; Wesselski Mönchslatein 60 No. 50.
T82.p: An empress lovesick for a particular man is to be cured by bathing in his blood.

T83.r: Lover drowned as he swims to see his mistress. *Von der Hagen I cxxviii; *Fb “svömme” III 695b; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Fox 202.
T83.p: Tragic love story in which a pair of lovers is kept apart and one dies, typically a young woman who drowns while trying to reach her lover across water.

T83.1.p: A young woman drowns while swimming toward her lover, because her brothers trick her by showing a false light to lead her astray.

T84.p: Two lovers are cruelly or deceitfully kept apart, so that their love is broken up by betrayal.

T85.p: A woman grieves for a lover who has died, remaining devoted to his memory.

T85.1.p: A woman, believing her lover is dead, builds a memorial monument to him and mourns in front of it.

T85.2.p: A princess hangs up her dead lover's weapons where she will always see them, as a constant reminder of him.

T85.3.r: *Belden PMLA XXXIII 327ff.; Boccaccio Decameron IV No. 5 (Lee 136); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
T85.3.p: A mistress keeps her murdered lover's skull in a flower pot and tends it out of grief.

T85.4.p: A grieving mistress keeps her dead lover's body preserved by embalming for many years.

T85.4.1.r: **A. Pauls Der Ring der Fastrada (Aachen, 1896); **K. Nyrop Fortids Sagn og Sange 1: Tove’s Tryllering (København, 1907); *Chauvin II 202 No. 48; *Moth Danske Studier (1915) 97ff.; *BP I 463f.; *G. Paris Journal des Savants Nov. 1896; Euphorion VI 186.
T85.4.1.p: A lover keeps his dead mistress's or wife's body from decaying with a magic ring; when the ring is removed, the body rots at once and he is cured of his love.

T86.r: *Chauvin V 107 No. 37; Heptameron Nos. 50, 70; Boccaccio Decameron IV No. 8 (Lee 140); Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T86.p: Lovers who die are buried together in the same grave, even though they were not able to be together in life.

T86.1.p: Rival suitors kill each other fighting over a woman's love; she dies of a broken heart, and all three are buried in the same grave.

T86.2.p: Two lovers die at the same moment, even though they are apart.

T86.3.p: A mistress throws herself into her dead lover's grave.

T86.4.p: A girl and boy promised to each other by their parents both die when they meet again after the girl has married someone else.

T87.p: Lovers who are forbidden to marry starve themselves to death.

T88.p: A woman struck by plague is deserted by her husband, and a former unsuccessful suitor seeks her out and she dies in his arms.

T88.1.p: A love continues on even after one of the lovers has married someone else.

T89.p: A miscellaneous group of motifs about tragic love that do not fit the more specific categories.

T89.1.p: A woman falls in love with a warrior who is dying from his wounds.

T89.1.1.p: A princess is married to a prince who is mortally wounded, and the two are left alone to die in the jungle.

T89.2.p: A woman gives up her own life to save the man she loves.

T90.p: A general heading for miscellaneous motifs about love that do not fit the more specific love categories.

T91.p: A general heading for love stories in which the lovers are of unequal status, age, wealth, or nature.

T91.1.r: See references to G530.2. Icelandic: De la Saussaye 337, *Boberg; Irish myth: *Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T91.1.p: A giant's daughter falls in love with a hero.

T91.1.1.p: A giant's daughter who loves a hero bears his child.

T91.2.p: A mortal falls in love with a devil, or a devil falls in love with a mortal.

T91.2.1.r: (Cf. G303.9.4.7.) Child V 283; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 368*f., 3265.
T91.2.1.p: A devil wants to become a maiden's lover.

T91.3.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 23.
T91.3.p: A mortal falls in love with a supernatural being.

T91.3.1.p: A supernatural lover does a girl's household chores.

T91.3.2.p: A goddess falls in love with a mortal man.

T91.3.3.p: A god falls in love with a mortal.

T91.3.3.1.p: A god falls in love with a woman of low caste.

T91.4.p: Lovers who differ greatly in age.

T91.4.1.p: A married woman of mature years falls in love with a young, inexperienced man.

T91.4.1.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 860.
T91.4.1.1.p: An old teacher wants to marry his young female pupil.

T91.5.p: Lovers of different wealth, where one is rich and the other poor.

T91.5.1.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 54 No. 405A*; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 247 No. 192.
T91.5.1.p: A rich girl falls in love with a poor boy.

T91.5.1.1.p: A merchant's daughter becomes intimate with a slave.

T91.6.p: Lovers of different rank, where one is noble and the other common.

T91.6.1.p: A person of low birth falls in love with a king or queen.

T91.6.1.1.p: A low-born man who has fallen in love with a queen is asked by her whom he loves, and he answers by holding up a mirror to her, showing that she is the one he loves.

T91.6.2.r: (Cf. L162, T121.8.) Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1185.
T91.6.2.p: A king or prince falls in love with a woman of low social rank.

T91.6.2.0.1.p: A king desires another man's wife, who is one of his subjects.

T91.6.3.p: A prince falls in love with the daughter of one of his chief advisers.

T91.6.3.1.p: A prince falls in love with the daughter of a merchant who had been abandoned in the jungle as a baby.

T91.6.4.r: (Cf. L161.) *Type 314; *Boje 74ff.; Penzer V 250, VIII 115ff.; Krappe “The Legends of Amicus and Amelius and of King Horn” Leuvensche Bijdragen XVI (1924) 14—17; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “jardinier”; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 348ff.
T91.6.4.p: A princess falls in love with a boy of low social rank.

T91.6.4.1.r: Dickson 133 n. 109; English: Wells 85 (The Sowdone of Babylone).
T91.6.4.1.p: The daughter of a sultan falls in love with a knight who has been captured and brought to her as a prisoner.

T91.6.4.1.1.p: A princess falls in love with a knight, and after her husband dies she marries him.

T91.6.4.1.2.p: The daughter of a hostile Amazon falls in love with a hero who is her mother's enemy.

T91.6.4.2.p: A princess falls in love with a king who has been reduced to working as a slave.

T91.6.4.3.p: A princess runs away with a hunchback to be with him.

T91.7.p: A miscellaneous group of love stories in which the lovers are of unequal social standing.

T91.7.1.p: A Brahmin man, of the highest caste, falls in love with a washerwoman.

T91.7.2.p: A person falls in love with someone from a different caste.

T92.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.
T92.p: Two or more suitors compete for the same person in love, creating a rivalry.

T92.0.1.p: A girl is promised to three different suitors, and unable to choose among them or settle the dispute, she eats poison and dies.

T92.1.p: The love triangle plot, in which two men love the same woman or two women love the same man, and the ways such rivalries are resolved.

T92.1.1.p: A young wife of an old man, often a king, loves or is loved by a younger man.

T92.1.2.p: A wife who is ready to be unfaithful to her husband but has not yet done so.

T92.2.r: All die of despair. *Chauvin V 110 No. 44.
T92.2.p: Three people are each in love with another in a chain: a girl loves a boy, the boy loves a singing girl, and the singing girl loves the first girl.

T92.3.p: A girl who has been rescued by one man leaves him and runs off with a younger man she loves more.

T92.3.1.p: A girl who has been rescued by one man leaves him and elopes with his friend.

T92.4.r: Italian: L. de Francia Novellino (Torino, 1930) Gaulteruzzi MS No. 99, Rotunda.
T92.4.p: A girl runs away with the wrong man by mistake instead of her chosen lover. The preferred suitor catches up with them, finds them asleep and waits for them to wake; but he falls asleep himself, and when he wakes they have gone.

T92.4.1.p: The hero falls asleep while his sweetheart is being married to another man.

T92.4.2.p: A letter is forged so that the girl is tricked into eloping with a false lover.

T92.4.3.p: In the dark of night a trickster elopes with the girl in place of her chosen lover, who was expected.

T92.5.p: A lover kills his rival who is his own brother.

T92.6.p: A mother and her daughter are rivals for the same lover.

T92.7.p: Two rival lovers fight each other in combat for the same girl.

T92.8.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
T92.8.p: Two sisters are both in love with the same man.

T92.9.p: A father and his son are rivals for the love of the same woman.

T92.9.1.p: A father is killed by his son, or a son by his father, because they are rivals for the same girl's love.

T92.10.p: A man's rival in love is killed.

T92.11.p: Several men compete for the same girl.

T92.11.1.p: Rival suitors cause each other trouble or embarrassment and so defeat each other.

T92.12.p: Two smiths are rivals for the love of the same girl.

T92.12.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1693A*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 1631*.
T92.12.1.p: A tailor and a smith are rivals for a girl. The tailor says the smith is blind, and the smith says the tailor is a fool. At the church wedding the smith drops a hot piece of iron into the tailor's boot.

T92.13.p: An older warrior is chosen as a suitor over younger men.

T92.14.p: Three lovers mourn a dead girl in different ways: one throws himself onto her funeral pyre, another gathers her ashes and vows to sit on them for life, and the third becomes a fakir (ascetic).

T93.p: What becomes of a lover whose love has been rejected or frustrated.

T93.1.r: (Cf. F567.) *Dickson 116 n. 44; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T93.1.p: A rejected lover goes off to live as a wild man in the forest, cut off from society.

T93.2.r: (Cf. V472.) Heptameron No. 64, 19; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
T93.2.p: A rejected lover withdraws from the world and becomes a hermit.

T93.2.1.p: A lover who cannot marry the beloved takes religious orders, becoming a friar, while the beloved becomes a nun.

T93.3.p: A rejected lover takes his own life out of despair.

T93.4.p: A disappointed lover buys poison to kill the girl, but the druggist sells him a sleeping potion instead; she wakes up and they are reconciled.

T93.5.p: A tragic romance between a fairy woman (pari) and a mortal man: they never meet again and wander the earth searching for each other.

T95.p: A lover is opposed by the relatives of the woman he loves.

T95.0.1.p: A princess falls in love with the enemy of her father.

T95.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; English: Child V 496 s.v. “Slaughter”; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
T95.1.p: A lover kills his lady's relatives in a fight.

T96.r: Boccaccio Decameron Book V (Lee 157ff.); Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T96.p: Lovers who have been separated by many adventures are finally reunited.

T97.p: A father refuses to let his daughter marry the man she wants.

T99.p: Miscellaneous additional motifs about love that do not fit the earlier categories.

T99.1.p: A man dies from having too many women, from exhaustion of his lovemaking.

T99.2.p: A girl is willing to marry her lover even though he has been mutilated or maimed.

T100.r: *E. Westermarck The History of Human Marriage (2 vols. London, 1925); Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 1522; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
T100.p: General heading for tales and motifs about marriage.

T102.p: A hero comes back after long absence and marries the first girl he loved.

T104.p: A foreign king goes to war to force the marriage of a princess to him.

T104.1.p: A rejected suitor makes war on the king who turned him down.

T104.2.p: The winner of a war demands the defeated king's daughter, or widow, in marriage.

T110.p: A marriage that is strange or out of the ordinary in some way.

T111.r: *Type 425; *Tegethoff 16; Krappe MLR XXIV (1929) 200ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
T111.p: A human marries a supernatural being such as a god, spirit, or otherworldly creature. This is the general heading for such unions.

T111.0.1.r: *Holmström Svanjungfrumotivet 11ff.; Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. 404*, 423*; India: Thompson-Balys; Mono-Alu: Wheeler Nos. 17, 35.
T111.0.1.p: A mortal man takes supernatural wives who later vanish and leave him.

T111.0.2.p: A supernatural wife can be called back to her husband by ringing a bell.

T111.1.r: Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 13, *Cross; Greek: cf. the various love affairs of Zeus with mortal maidens; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hindu: Tawney I 256, 302, 335, 351, 560f.; Maori: Dixon 57.

T111.1.1.p: A maiden chooses as her husband a god who has disguised himself as a man.

T111.1.2.r: Korean: Zong in-Sob 137 No. 63; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 181f.
T111.1.2.p: A man marries the daughter of a god.

T111.2.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 110; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 60 No. 12, (Congo): Weeks 206 No. 3, (Angola): Chatelain 131 No. 13.
T111.2.p: A woman from the sky-world marries a mortal man.

T111.2.1.p: A hero marries a star who takes the form of a girl.

T111.2.1.1.p: The star-wife, who is a star in girl's form, bears a human child.

T111.2.2.r: (Cf. A753.1.) Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 29, (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 307, (Cumberland Sound): ibid. 198, (Greenland): Holm 47, Rasmussen III 307; S. A. Indian (Viracocha): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 550.

T111.2.3.r: S. A. Indian (Warrau): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 145.
T111.2.3.p: The sun has a human woman as his wife.

T111.3.p: A man marries a woman who has come out of an egg.

T111.4.p: A god takes as lovers eighteen giantesses.

T111.5.r: Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 183, 209, (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 151, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 170—3; Koryak: Jochelson JE VI 154, 201, 227.

T113.p: A man marries a woman who, by night, makes him alive, but by day he is dead. The marriage has a deathlike or enchanted pattern in which the husband's state changes between day and night.

T113.1.p: A sorceress marries a man each morning and by evening turns him into some kind of animal.

T115.p: A man marries the daughter of an ogre, a man-eating giant.

T117.p: A person marries an inanimate object.

T117.2.p: A girl is married to a sword, so the marriage is with an inanimate weapon rather than a person.

T117.3.p: A girl is married to a drum, so the bride's husband is an inanimate musical instrument.

T117.4.p: A girl is married to an idol, a carved or worshipped image of a god.

T117.5.r: Frazer Golden Bough I 195f.; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 304 n. 109o.
T117.5.p: A person marries a tree, which serves as the spouse.

T117.5.1.p: The tree-spouse is a tree by day and turns into a man at night, so the marriage is partly with a tree and partly with a human husband.

T117.6.p: A person marries a flower, which serves as the spouse.

T117.7.p: A person marries a gourd, a hard-shelled fruit or vine vessel, which serves as the spouse.

T117.8.p: A person marries a doll, a toy figure in human form.

T117.9.p: A person marries a river, which serves as the spouse.

T117.10.p: A plant takes the form of a woman and becomes a man's wife.

T117.11.p: A person marries a statue, a carved figure of a person.

T118.r: *Types 306, 506; *Liljeblad passim; *BP III 83; *Kittredge Harvard Studies and Notes in Philology VIII 250; Irish myth: *Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
T118.p: A girl, or sometimes a man, is married to or falls in love with a monster.

T118.1.p: The monster husband cannot be seen by his wife, so he is invisible.

T118.2.p: A dragon's daughter marries a poor orphan boy.

T121.r: Child V 500 s.v. “Unequal”; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
T121.p: A marriage takes place between partners of very different social ranks.

T121.1.r: English: Wells 60 (Syre Gowene and the Carle of Carelyle).
T121.1.p: A knight marries a peasant girl of low social standing.

T121.2.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 57; Italian Novella: Rotunda.

T121.3.p: A princess marries a man of the court who is of lower rank than she is.

T121.3.1.p: A princess marries a man of humble, low birth.

T121.4.p: A ruler marries a noblewoman who is a fugitive, on the run from her own people or from danger.

T121.5.p: A wealthy girl marries a man who is both physically deformed and poor, though he is a learned thinker. The match goes against social expectation.

T121.5.1.p: A princess marries a holy man (a saint). The match is unusual because of the gap in status between them.

T121.5.2.p: A wealthy girl marries a fakir, a wandering ascetic or holy beggar. The match crosses class and social lines.

T121.6.p: A man marries a woman he owns as a bondmaid, a female servant or slave.

T121.7.p: A rich girl marries a man who works as her servant, so the marriage crosses class lines.

T121.8.r: (Cf. L162, T91.6.2.) Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 938, II 1091.
T121.8.p: A king or wealthy man marries a commoner, a girl of humble origin.

T121.8.1.p: A childless king marries a beggar woman, hoping she will bear him a son.

T122.p: A widow who is reluctant to remarry is ordered by a queen, in a letter, to marry the man who carries it, a suitor chosen for her by royal command.

T125.p: A lazy boy and a hardworking girl are paired in marriage, so that each partner is mismatched to the other's character.

T125.1.p: A fool is given a clever wife, and a lame man is given a hardworking wife. Each marriage pairs a poor trait with a good one.

T125.2.p: A blind girl marries a lame man. Each is disabled in a different way.

T126.p: A marriage between unlikely or supernatural partners, such as beings that are not ordinary humans.

T126.1.p: The Earth Mother, a personification of the earth, marries an ogre, a giant man-eating monster.

T126.2.p: A mountain marries a cockle-shell, an unlikely pairing of a huge object with a tiny one.

T126.3.p: The earth marries the sky, a cosmic pairing of the two great parts of the world.

T130.p: General heading for customs and rules that surround marriage in various cultures.

T131.p: Rules or limits that a society places on who may marry whom.

T131.0.1.p: A princess is free to choose any man she likes as her husband, with no restriction from others.

T131.0.1.1.p: A father promises that his daughter may marry only the man she herself chooses.

T131.1.p: A marriage is allowed only if a relative gives consent, so a family member's approval is required.

T131.1.1.r: Child I 142ff.; Heptameron No. 40; Icelandic: *Boberg; Japanese: Ikeda.
T131.1.1.p: A brother's permission is required before his sister may marry.

T131.1.2.p: A father's permission is required before his son or daughter may marry.

T131.1.2.1.p: A girl is required to marry the man her father chooses for her.

T131.1.2.2.p: A king selects a husband for his daughter by looking at pictures of possible suitors.

T131.1.2.3.p: A father orders his son to end all contact with the person he loves.

T131.1.2.4.p: A son refuses to marry the bride his father has chosen for him.

T131.1.3.p: A couple marries despite the objections of their parents.

T131.2.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 566; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Rittershaus No. 2; Indonesia: Pleyte Bataksche Vertellingen 184f., Wilken Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land-, en Volkenkunde van Nederlandsch-Indië I 142; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 323.
T131.2.p: A younger child may not marry before an older sibling does.

T131.3.p: The eldest daughter agrees to marry a man only if he also marries all her younger sisters.

T131.4.p: A widow is forbidden to marry again.

T131.5.p: People must marry outside their own group, such as their clan or kin group.

T131.5.1.p: Marriage within a clan is allowed because the tribe itself began through incest.

T131.6.p: A girl agrees to marry only on the condition that she will be her husband's only wife.

T131.7.p: A king may not marry a girl who has previously been another man's wife.

T131.8.p: Belonging to a different religion prevents two people from marrying.

T131.9.p: A Brahmin man may marry women from any of the four Hindu castes.

T132.1.p: A girl is fed heavily before her wedding so she will be plumper.

T132.2.p: Parents work as servants to earn the money needed to pay for their child's wedding.

T133.p: Journey taken to reach the wedding.

T133.1.p: A loyal servant goes along with the bride when she travels to her new home for the wedding.

T133.2.p: A royal bride is escorted to her husband's kingdom by an official envoy.

T133.3.p: Drummers beat drums in front of the bride as she goes to her wedding.

T133.4.p: The bridegroom comes with his followers to collect the bride for the wedding.

T133.5.p: The groom rides out on horseback to bring the bride home.

T133.6.p: The groom's mother visits the future bride and places the betrothal ring on her finger.

T134.p: Rules about how the engaged couple must behave before the wedding ceremony.

T134.1.p: The bride and groom are forbidden to see each other before the wedding.

T134.2.p: The betrothed people do not see each other until the night of the wedding.

T134.3.p: A man who has already been married helps the groom get dressed for his wedding.

T135.p: The wedding ceremony itself and the ways a marriage is made formal.

T135.1.p: The couple declares at the wedding, "You are mine and I am yours."

T135.2.p: Touching each other's private parts is treated as making a binding marriage agreement.

T135.3.p: The marriage is performed with one or both parties absent, represented by someone else.

T135.3.1.p: A sword and a shield stand in for the absent person at the wedding ceremony.

T135.4.p: The groom's sword marks the bride's forehead with vermilion, and this serves as the wedding ceremony.

T135.5.p: The couple is married by exchanging garlands with each other.

T135.6.p: The couple is married at a festival where they drink together.

T135.7.p: The bride must have a man, usually her father or brother, to give her away at the wedding.

T135.8.p: Two or more weddings happen at the same time as the ending of a story.

T135.9.p: A wedding is held as a formal religious ceremony inside a church.

T135.10.p: As part of the wedding rite, the couple walks around a fire, a pillar, or a similar object.

T135.11.p: As part of the wedding ceremony, the bride and groom share a drink from one cup.

T135.12.p: Before the wedding, the bodies of the bride and groom are smeared with turmeric and mustard oil.

T135.13.p: During the wedding, the bride and groom look into a large mirror while an elderly relative knocks their heads together.

T135.14.p: A canopy is held or raised over the bride and groom during the wedding.

T135.15.p: During the wedding ceremony, a glass is broken.

T136.p: A general heading for the events and extras that go along with a wedding.

T136.1.p: A feast is held to celebrate the wedding.

T136.2.r: *Crane Vitry 249 No. 265; Herbert III 22; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 1649, III 385f., IV 168f.; Frazer Golden Bough I 254; Mannhardt Wald und Feldkulte I 222.
T136.2.p: Rice is thrown at the couple at a wedding.

T136.3.p: Entertainment and amusements are provided at the wedding.

T136.3.2.p: Songs in praise of the marriage are sung at the wedding feast.

T136.4.p: Guests give gifts to the couple at the wedding.

T136.4.1.p: The couple receives gifts in a special ceremony in which the bride sits on a bridal bench.

T136.4.2.p: Guests give departing gifts to the couple or family after the wedding.

T136.4.3.p: The bride throws presents out among the groom's relatives.

T137.p: A general heading for customs that take place after the wedding.

T137.1.p: Someone gives advice to the bride as she leaves her family to go to her new home.

T137.2.p: After the ceremony, the bride and groom are escorted to the bridal bed.

T137.2.1.p: As the couple enter the groom's house, the bride and groom each touch the hearthstones and step over the threshold with one foot, as a wedding custom. The rite is performed as they are led to the bridal bed.

T137.3.p: After the wedding ceremony, the groom is welcomed into the women's quarters to share the wedding breakfast with the bride.

T137.4.p: The groom joins the bride's family and becomes one of its members.

T137.5.p: After the wedding, the groom and his party go to fetch the bride (and her party) to bring her to his home.

T137.6.p: The bride travels to her husband's home with attendants accompanying her.

T141.p: A bride is handed over or given from one man to another.

T141.1.p: A dying man gives his bride to his brother to marry.

T141.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 223, (Greenland): Holm 75.
T141.2.p: Two men swap their wives with each other.

T141.3.p: A hero who has won a bride gives her to another man.

T143.p: Marriages in which one or both partners are still infants.

T145.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Duala): Lederbogen Märchen 82, (Fang): Trilles Legends 263f.
T145.p: A man has more than one wife at the same time.

T145.0.1.p: A man has several wives at once (the usual form of polygamy).

T145.1.p: A man marries five women, each of whom has a separate set of household duties.

T145.1.1.p: A man insists that he needs seven women to be his wives.

T145.1.2.p: A man has seven wives, and each has him one day of the week.

T145.1.3.p: A man is married to several sisters at the same time.

T145.2.p: A man takes a second wife because his first wife cannot have children.

T145.3.p: The two wives of a king compete to see who can brew the better ale.

T145.4.p: A man's two wives each claim a part of his body as their own, and they torment him.

T145.5.p: A man's two wives pull him down the stairs.

T145.6.p: A man who has several wives must love them all equally, not just one of them.

T145.7.p: A man has two wives: the older, first one is plain but hardworking, and the second is beautiful but lazy.

T145.8.p: A man takes several wives so that if the head wife does wrong, he can quickly replace her with another.

T146.p: Polyandry: a woman has two or more husbands at the same time.

T146.1.p: Several men marry the same woman.

T146.2.p: A woman needs thirty men as husbands, and she is able to take them all.

T147.p: People choose their marriage partners or arrange their marriages at a yearly festival.

T148.p: Matriarchy: a society in which women hold the power and descent or inheritance is traced through them.

T148.1.p: A son is named after his mother rather than his father.

T150.p: Things that happen at weddings, including unusual or magical events during the wedding celebration.

T151.r: *Type 300, 301; *Loomis White Magic 120; Irish myth: *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 94; English: Wells 135 (Sir Degare); Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T151.p: A person wins a year's delay before having to marry someone they do not want to marry.

T151.0.1.p: A captive maiden tricks her captor by giving him a quest and promising to marry him only when it is completed, which buys her time.

T151.0.2.p: A father who gives his daughter in marriage sets a condition that the son-in-law may not treat her as his wife for one year.

T151.1.p: A person gains a six-month delay before having to marry someone they do not want to marry.

T151.2.p: A person gains a thirty-day delay before having to marry someone they do not want to marry.

T151.3.p: A person gains some other delay, such as three months or two years, before having to marry someone they do not want to marry.

T152.p: A bride is accidentally wounded on the way home from her wedding and dies from a wound caused by the bridegroom's sword.

T153.p: A bridegroom is killed on his way to meet his bride.

T154.p: A cruel stepmother casts a spell on her stepdaughter on the eve of her wedding.

T155.r: (Cf. D113.1.) Dh III 454; Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 14 No. 75, XXXIII 53 No. 75; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 130 No. 73, 145 No. 38; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3674; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 63 No. 160.
T155.p: An old beggar changes a wedding party into wolves.

T156.p: A hero agrees to marry a girl so she can escape an unwanted marriage, promising to give her up the next day after posting a large bond. He then tricks his way into the money and keeps her as his wife.

T156.1.p: A man marries a woman for one night so that his child will be the heir of a warrior who is destined to be killed in battle the next day.

T157.p: A chieftain's betrothed falls in love with another man at the betrothal feast, drugs everyone with a sleeping potion, and elopes with him.

T160.p: General heading for motifs about the consummation, meaning the first sexual union, of a marriage.

T161.r: Liebrecht Orient und Occident II 541f., Liebrecht 94, 416; Herrmann Saxo II 324; *Hertz Abhandlungen 207ff.; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 746; *Wesselski Archiv Orientální I 82f.—Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 140, *Cross; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 319 No. 21; French: Sébillot France IV 285; Jewish: *bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 363, *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
T161.p: A lord claims the right to sleep with a subject's bride on the wedding night before the husband does.

T161.0.1.p: A king takes the virginity of every twelve-year-old girl in his realm.

T161.1.p: A lover is permitted to sleep with a woman during the first few nights after she has married someone else.

T162.p: A feast called "bedding and handspreading" is held before a marriage is consummated.

T165.r: (Cf. C117.) *Fb “brud” IV 64b; *DeVries Zs. f. deutsche Philologie LIII 276f.; Hdwb: d. Abergl. III 739; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
T165.p: A bride is allowed to stay a virgin for three days after the wedding before the marriage is consummated.

T165.1.r: DeVries Zs. f. deutsche Philologie LIII 277.
T165.1.p: The marriage is not consummated until a dream reveals that the family's future has been secured.

T165.2.p: A full year passes between the wedding ceremony and the consummation of the marriage.

T165.3.p: The marriage is not consummated until twenty-four hours have passed.

T165.4.p: The bride and groom are kept apart on their wedding night.

T165.5.p: As a trick, a man asks for three years to pass before the marriage is consummated.

T165.6.p: The marriage is not consummated until the couple returns home.

T165.7.p: For the first six months, a prince's bride only sits for an hour or two in his house and is not otherwise with him.

T166.p: A frightened bride refuses to consummate the marriage until a judge orders her to submit in court.

T166.1.p: A bride refuses to sleep with her groom because she finds him ugly.

T166.2.p: The bridegroom must be taught how to have sexual intercourse.

T171.r: *Type 559; *BP II 454; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 5; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 411ff.
T171.p: A magic force drives the groom out of the bridal chamber so he cannot consummate the marriage, usually by hornets or wasps.

T172.p: The husband faces dangers in the bridal chamber on the wedding night.

T172.0.1.r: See references to F547.1.1, F582, F582.1. *Types 506—08; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T172.0.1.p: Every husband dies on the wedding night, so the bride is left widowed before the marriage is consummated.

T172.1.p: The bridal bed chamber is found full of coiled snakes, a danger that threatens the husband on his wedding night.

T172.2.r: (Cf. B176.1.) *Types 507AB, 516; Liljeblad passim; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 9; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T172.2.p: A magic dragon or serpent invades the bridal chamber on the wedding night and threatens the couple.

T172.2.1.r: (Or otherwise renders her innocuous to the bridegroom.) *Type 506—08.
T172.2.1.p: A grateful dead man comes back to help and kills the princess's monstrous husband, who is the dragon or serpent that invaded the bridal chamber.

T172.3.p: The bride's father, who is a monster, tries to kill the husband on the wedding night but is defeated.

T173.p: A bride who tries to kill her husband, a deadly or murderous wife.

T173.1.p: A strong bride tries to smother her husband in bed.

T173.2.r: *Encyc. Britannica 13 s.v. “Danaus”; Frazer Apollodorus I 143 n. 1; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 306A*; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T173.2.p: Hostile brides kill their husbands in the bridal bed.

T175.r: magic horse, poison, enchanted clothes, etc. *Type 516; **Rösch FFC LXXVII 123ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 9; India: *Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 155 No. 68.
T175.p: Magical dangers of various kinds threaten the newly married couple.

T175.1.p: Furniture is arranged by a jealous rival so that it will fall on the bridal couple.

T177.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I Nos. 7, 9. See also all references to Forgotten Fiancée (D2003).
T177.p: A bridegroom is magically compelled to leave his bride.

T181.p: A husband who is dangerous to his wife.

T182.p: A person dies as a result of sexual intercourse.

T190.p: Miscellaneous motifs concerning marriage that do not fit the more specific headings.

T192.p: A person is forced into marriage against their will.

T200.p: General motifs about how life goes for people after they have married.

T201.p: Lovers who live together happily become unhappy as soon as they marry, so marriage ruins their friendship.

T202.p: A married couple in which the wife is blind and the husband is deaf, so each is unable to notice the other's failings.

T203.p: Keeping peace in a marriage is valued more highly than telling the truth.

T210.p: Being faithful to one's spouse within marriage.

T210.1.p: A wife who remains loyal to her husband and does not betray him or stray from the marriage.

T210.2.p: A husband who remains loyal to his wife and does not betray her or stray from the marriage.

T211.r: Herrmann Saxo II 94; Icelandic: *Boberg; Korean: Zong in-Sob 30 No. 13.
T211.p: A spouse's loyalty to the marriage continues even beyond death, shown in various ways after the partner dies.

T211.1.p: A wife dies in place of her husband so that his death is put off for a time.

T211.1.1.p: A woman drowns herself as an offering to the water-gods so that her husband's boat will not capsize.

T211.1.2.p: A husband is told by augurs that his wife will die if he saves himself from a serpent, so he lets himself be bitten and dies.

T211.1.3.p: A wife offers to sacrifice her right arm so that her husband will return safely.

T211.1.4.p: A female deer offers herself in place of her mate, who has been caught by a hunter. The hunter, moved by her sacrifice, releases both deer.

T211.2.p: A wife kills herself when her husband dies.

T211.2.1.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 375 n. 3 (Evadne); Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T211.2.1.p: A wife throws herself onto her husband's funeral pyre to be burned with him.

T211.2.1.1.p: A wife chooses to be burned with her husband even though she was forced to marry him, and she had helped to plan his revenge.

T211.2.2.p: A wife promises that she will die along with her husband.

T211.3.p: A husband and wife both kill themselves so that they will not be separated by death.

T211.3.1.p: A husband kills himself by falling on his sword when his wife dies.

T211.3.2.p: A wife hangs herself because her husband has been killed.

T211.4.p: A dead spouse's body is kept and not buried or given up after death.

T211.4.1.r: Type 612; Wesselski Märchen 188, 191; BP I 463f.; Moth Danske Studier (1915) 97ff.; Pauls Der Ring der Fastrada (Aachen, 1896); Chauvin II 201ff.; Cowell Jataka II 108.
T211.4.1.p: A husband keeps his dead wife's body and does not bury it.

T211.4.2.p: A wife keeps her dead husband's body and does not bury it.

T211.4.2.1.p: A wife refuses to hand over her dead husband's body to the God of Death.

T211.5.p: A man withdraws from society to live as a hermit after his wife dies.

T211.6.r: *Type 65; BP I 362; *Taylor JAFL XLVI 78; Fb “ræv” III 113b.
T211.6.p: A widowed vixen turns down suitors who do not look like her dead husband, showing she still mourns him and wants no replacement.

T211.7.p: A girl who is forced to marry while her sweetheart is away stays faithful to her husband. When she refuses her former fiancé a kiss, he drops dead; she then dies over his body at his funeral.

T211.8.p: A wife refuses to deceive her husband, even when it would let her be with the man she loves.

T211.9.p: A person grieves so intensely over the death of a spouse that the grief becomes excessive or dangerous.

T211.9.1.p: A wife dies from grief when she learns that her husband has died.

T211.9.1.1.p: A wife faints and dies on realizing that her husband is dead.

T211.9.2.p: A man takes his own life out of grief for his dead wife.

T211.9.2.1.p: A grieving man goes to die at the place where his wife's body lies.

T212.p: A loving married couple who are separated die because they cannot bear being apart.

T212.1.p: A husband who has died is brought back to life because of his wife's constant faithfulness.

T213.p: A husband or wife becomes sick because of being separated from the spouse.

T215.p: A married couple stay loyal to each other through hardship and misfortune.

T215.1.p: A wife carries her crippled husband on her back so that he can beg for them both.

T215.2.p: A wife offers her starving husband or father milk from her own breasts to keep him alive.

T215.3.p: A husband feeds his starving wife with his own flesh and blood to keep her alive.

T215.4.r: Von der Hagen I cxxiv; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
T215.4.p: A wife gouges out one of her own eyes to show she shares her husband's misfortune. He has lost an eye in a tournament and is ashamed to face her; she shows that his injury makes no difference to her love.

T215.5.p: A fugitive goes back to his family so that they can collect the reward for capturing him.

T215.6.p: A woman swims every night to her imprisoned husband and arranges his escape. She refuses the advances of a treacherous suitor.

T215.7.p: A wife travels with her sick husband for years, trying to find a cure for him.

T215.7.1.r: Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1060.
T215.7.1.p: A wife alone does not abandon her husband who has leprosy, while others do.

T215.8.p: A wife cuts off and sells her hair to get food for her husband, who is starving, showing she stays loyal to him in hard times.

T216.p: A wife faithfully carries her ugly, cursed husband on her back in a basket, staying with him despite his loathsome form.

T217.p: A wife refuses to be unfaithful even though she knows her husband has been unfaithful to her.

T221.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
T221.p: A wife's innocence proves her faithfulness: she never told her husband when he had bad breath, because she thought men liked it as she did, showing she has never known another man.

T222.p: A wife covers up her husband's affair from the emperor and even gives shelter to his mistress.

T224.p: A wife disguised in fine clothes tempts her husband, who refuses to touch any woman but his own wife; she then changes back into her old clothes to reveal herself.

T230.p: Husbands and wives who are unfaithful to each other in marriage.

T230.1.p: A husband and wife each suspect the other of infidelity over the slightest hint.

T230.2.p: An unfaithful wife drives her husband insane.

T231.p: A widow who is not faithful to her dead husband's memory and quickly looks for a new partner.

T231.1.p: A widow gets engaged to a new suitor at her husband's own funeral.

T231.2.p: A widow fans her husband's grave to dry the earth so she can remarry sooner, since she does not want to wait until the body is cold.

T231.3.p: A widow is ready to marry a messenger who brings news of her husband's death, but the husband has only pretended to be dead to test her.

T231.3.1.p: A widow offers her city to the man who killed her husband if he will marry her.

T231.4.p: A widow's cold heartlessness drives away a new suitor: she obeys his order to knock out the teeth of her dead husband, and he flees, fearing she would treat him the same way when he died.

T231.5.p: A widow marries the man who killed her husband.

T232.r: (Deformed, mutilated, monstrous, or of different race.) *Penzer V 153 n. 1; Malone PMLA XLIII 418ff.; Strauch Enikels Weltchronik, lines 25177ff. — Irish myth: Cross; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Palestine: Schmidt-Kahle Volkserzählungen aus Palästina I 139ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 109; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 148.
T232.p: A wife leaves her husband for a lover who is not worthy of her.

T232.1.p: A woman has an affair with a leper.

T232.2.p: An adulterous wife chooses an ugly, loathsome man as her lover.

T232.3.p: An adulteress poisons her husband so she can be with a swineherd.

T232.4.p: A woman falls for a lover who is ugly, cruel, and mistreats her. She is drawn to him despite, or because of, his repulsive and abusive behavior.

T232.5.p: An unfaithful wife makes her lover pay her for the pleasure of sleeping with him.

T233.p: A wife who has been wronged by her husband goes back to him, and the husband is the one who has been wronged in the marriage.

T235.p: A husband disguises himself in another form in order to test whether his wife will remain faithful to him.

T236.p: A woman is attracted to an unknown knight at a tournament but loses interest when she learns he is her own husband.

T237.r: Irish myth: Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
T237.p: An old man has married a young wife who is unfaithful to him.

T238.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 51; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T238.p: A woman who is dying confesses on her deathbed that her children were fathered by other men. She kept this secret so her husband would not have to raise them.

T241.p: A woman who is unfaithful goes through a series of husbands, and each one fails to keep her under control.

T243.p: A husband and a lover fight each other over a kingdom and over the wife they both claim.

T244.p: A wife, angry that her husband has deserted her, tells an enemy where he is hiding.

T244.1.p: A wife, angry that her husband has deserted her, tells a hungry bear where he is hiding.

T245.p: A man is unfaithful to his wife even on their wedding night.

T247.p: A person takes an object from the lover's place as proof that the infidelity has been discovered.

T247.1.p: A husband, on finding his wife and her lover together, leaves a wooden sword in the lover's scabbard as a sign that he knows of the affair.

T249.p: A miscellaneous group of tales about unfaithfulness in marriage that do not fit the more specific categories.

T249.1.p: A wife found guilty of adultery takes her own life.

T249.2.p: A king and queen are each unfaithful to the other.

T250.p: A general group of tales about the typical traits and behavior of wives and husbands.

T251.r: *Penzer II 159f.; Hanna Lindberg “The Shrew”, argbiggans typ i den Engelska Literaturen intill Shakespeare (Tavastehus, 1900); India: *Thompson-Balys.
T251.p: A wife who is nagging, quarrelsome, and hard to live with.

T251.0.1.p: A man is thrown out of heaven for the foolishness of marrying a second time.

T251.0.2.p: A man, having heard about Christ's sufferings, concludes that Christ could not understand suffering because he never married. The joke is that a shrewish wife is the real torment.

T251.0.3.p: A judge scolds a man for having married several times, and the man answers that he was always searching for a good wife.

T251.1.p: A man escapes or avoids a bad-tempered, quarrelsome wife, sometimes by extreme means.

T251.1.1.r: *Type 1164; **Axon The Story of Belfagor in Literature and Folklore (1902); *BP I 382, 388, IV 176 n. 1; *Prato RTP IV 174; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk.
