T251.1.1.p: A man lowers his shrewish wife into a well, and when he later pulls her out he raises a devil, who is glad to flee her. The man then scares the devil by telling him that the wife has escaped.

T251.1.1.1.p: A devil flees the shrewish wife and possesses a duke's body. He is driven out by being told that the wife is being sent for.

T251.1.2.p: A husband who has died would rather stay in Purgatory than return to his shrewish wife.

T251.1.2.1.p: A husband chooses to go to hell rather than join his shrewish wife in heaven.

T251.1.2.2.r: Bargain with the devil: should the latter not be able to endure life with his wife for three years, the man would be released from hell. The devil is the loser. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1164B*.
T251.1.2.2.p: A man in hell says life there is much better than life on earth with his wife.

T251.1.3.p: A man would rather stay transformed into a mule than live with his shrewish wife.

T251.1.4.p: A man forces the devil to take back the shrewish wife whom the devil had been given or had carried off.

T251.1.5.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 138; Mensa Philosophica No. 61; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T251.1.5.p: A minstrel throws his wife into the sea, because when ordered to throw heavy things overboard, her tongue proves the heaviest thing on board.

T251.1.6.p: A thief overhears two jealous wives quarrelling and, when brought before a judge, asks to be punished with anything except having two wives.

T251.2.r: *Types 900, 901; *BP I 443; **Philippson FFC L; *Wesselski Arlotto II 229 No. 95; *Gigas “Et eventyrs vandring” Litteratur og Historie (3e samling) (København, 1902); *Krappe Études ital. II 141ff.; *Wesselski Märchen 216 No. 24; Köhler-Bolte I 137; Chauvin II 155 No. 27.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T251.2.p: A husband tames a shrewish wife by outdoing her in shrewishness, so that she becomes obedient.

T251.2.1.p: A shrewish wife is tamed by setting another shrew against her, so that the two quarrel and she is cowed.

T251.2.2.p: A husband puts on armor and makes the household shout "Long live the Master!" He then takes off his breeches and dares his wife to put them on, establishing his authority at home.

T251.2.3.p: A wife becomes obedient after watching her husband kill a stubborn horse.

T251.2.3.1.p: A husband tries to reform his wife by killing a stubborn horse in front of her, but she thinks he has lost his mind and does not change her ways.

T251.2.4.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 904*; Russian: Andrejev No. 901I*; Prussian: Plenzat 49.
T251.2.4.p: A wicked queen is reformed: while she sleeps she is swapped places with a cobbler's wife, wakes thinking she is in hell, and is taught by the cobbler to obey and fear her husband.

T251.2.5.p: A shrewish wife, driven from home, runs to her husband when in danger and receives his protection, and she is a good wife afterwards.

T251.3.p: A nagging wife greets her husband, here St. Peter, at the back door with a broom handle to beat him.

T251.4.r: *Wesselski Arlotto II 258 No. 183; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 471; England: Baughman.
T251.4.p: Socrates, whose wife Xanthippe is a shrew, remarks "After thunder comes rain" as she empties slops over his head.

T251.5.r: (Cf. J1563.6, J1581.2, J2412.5.) Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 134; Mensa Philosophica No. 58.
T251.5.p: A shrewish, bad-tempered wife is finally tamed. Three remedies are tried in turn: the first two fail, and the third, a cure from the last of them, succeeds.

T251.6.r: Type 1366*; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 141 No. 1705.
T251.6.p: A henpecked husband, hiding under the table, declares that a man still has a man's heart, that he is not as meek as his wife thinks.

T251.7.p: A husband refuses to go looking for his shrewish wife after she has run away from him, glad to be rid of her.

T251.8.p: Every morning a shrewish wife greets her husband by hitting him, giving him a beating to start the day.

T251.9.p: A husband is comforted when he sees a woman who is even more shrewish than his own wife.

T251.10.p: A wife beats her husband and consumes everything he earns, leaving him with nothing.

T251.11.p: A holy man (fakir) is grateful for his shrewish wife, whom he sees as a thorn in his flesh that keeps him from neglecting religious duty and righteous living.

T252.p: A wife who domineers over her husband and insists on controlling the household.

T252.1.p: A search for a man who is able to rule his wife fails; no such man can be found.

T252.2.r: (Cf. J21.16, J130.) *Type 670; **Aarne FFC XV 49ff.; Fb “kok” IV 272b; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
T252.2.p: A cock teaches a henpecked husband how to get the upper hand over his wife.

T252.2.1.r: Follows its example. Scala Celi 7a No. 40; Oesterley No. 82; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
T252.2.1.p: A king watches a male stork kill his unfaithful wife, and learns from the example how a husband should deal with a wife who betrays him.

T252.2.2.p: A monkey, jackal or similar animal shows a husband how to rule his wife.

T252.2.2.1.r: Jackal: husbands ruled by their wives counted as women. India: Thompson-Balys.
T252.2.2.1.p: A king tells a jackal that his counting is wrong, since there are more men than women in the world.

T252.3.p: A wife threatens her husband with death unless he reveals his secrets to her.

T252.4.p: A prize is offered to any husband who can prove he rules his wife.

T252.4.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 753; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
T252.4.1.p: A man claims the prize, the boots, as ruler of his house, but he is too afraid of his wife to carry them home, in case he dirties his clean shirt and angers her.

T252.5.r: Wesselski Bebel II 148 No. 157; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 811.
T252.5.p: Men who are supposed to rule their households are asked to sing, but none in the congregation will; only the priest sings, and the next year he cannot, because he has taken a maidservant.

T252.6.p: A wife threatens to kill herself if she does not get her own way.

T252.7.p: An angry wife hits her husband on the head with a pot in front of a guest.

T253.p: A wife who constantly scolds and complains at her husband.

T253.1.p: A nagging wife badgers her husband until he is so miserable he decides to kill himself.

T253.2.p: A woman is told by someone wise that constant nagging will never make her husband good.

T253.3.p: A holy man composes a hymn to escape the miserable life he shares with his nagging wife.

T254.p: A wife who refuses to obey her husband, and the trouble that follows.

T254.1.r: Chauvin II 155 No. 27; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 38; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T254.1.p: A husband shows his wife a poison and warns her to avoid it; she eats it anyway and dies.

T254.2.p: A husband forbids his wife to ride the dog; she does it at once and is bitten.

T254.3.p: A man with an obedient wife stays young-looking, while one with a disobedient wife grows old.

T254.4.p: A man forbids his wife to open a chest; she opens it anyway, and a loaded crossbow inside kills her.

T254.5.p: A husband warns his wife not to go into an empty furnace; she goes in and it collapses on her.

T254.6.p: A disobedient wife is punished for not doing what her husband tells her.

T254.6.1.p: A wife refuses to bring her husband warm water and is beaten for it.

T255.p: A wife or husband who is stubbornly unwilling to give in during an argument.

T255.1.r: *Type 1365B; *Köhler-Bolte I 136; *Taylor Washington Univ. Studies IV 181 n. 28; *Crane Vitry 223 No. 222; Bédier Fabliaux (1895) 46ff.; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 595; Moe Samlede Skrifter I 209ff.: Spanish Exempla: Keller.
T255.1.p: In an argument, the stubborn wife is thrown into water, and as she sinks she mimes cutting with scissors, still refusing to yield.

T255.2.r: *Type 1365A; *Crane Vitry 225f. No. 227; Köhler-Bolte I 506 n. 1; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 270 No. 276; *Moe Samlede Skrifter I 212; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 142; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
T255.2.p: An obstinate wife falls into a stream, and her husband searches upstream for her, reasoning she would be too stubborn to float with the current.

T255.3.r: *Type 1365C; *Crane Vitry 222f. No. 221;. *Bédier Fabliaux 46; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 872; Herbert III 17; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T255.3.p: A wife calls her husband a lousy head and he throws her into a stream; as she sinks she makes the sign of cracking a louse.

T255.4.r: She jumps up and cries out “I eat two!” and everyone flees except a lame man who exclaims, “Poor me and the other one!” Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 123 No. 1365D*.
T255.4.p: A husband and wife argue over who gets the third egg; she pretends to die, and at her grave asks whether she may eat two of the three eggs, and he agrees.

T255.4.1.p: A stubborn wife insists on eating three of five eggs, refusing to share.

T255.5.p: A wife keeps serving a dish her husband hates; he pretends to like it so she will stop, and thus gets rid of it.

T255.6.p: A stubborn wife refuses to lift the lid off a boiling kettle and is beaten by her husband.

T255.7.p: A man tells his wife he dreamed a wolf would attack her; she ignores him, and the dream comes true.

T256.p: A wife or husband who is constantly quarrelsome and argues with the spouse.

T256.0.1.p: The couple's constant quarrelling is explained by their having been a tiger and a dog in an earlier life.

T256.1.p: A quarrelsome wife is cured of her temper when her silent husband refuses to argue with her and so defeats her.

T256.2.p: A medicine is prescribed to stop quarrelling: whenever the husband is angry, the wife must take a dose and hold it in her mouth for ten minutes.

T256.3.p: A quarrelsome wife is corrected by being given a good beating.

T257.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T257.p: A wife or husband who is jealous of the spouse's attentions or interests.

T257.0.1.p: Heavenly maidens (celestial women) are never jealous.

T257.1.p: A wife is jealous of a beautiful maid living in her house, fearing the maid will attract her husband.

T257.1.1.p: A king's wives are jealous because he pays attention to a pet animal.

T257.2.p: Rival wives, married to the same man, are jealous of one another.

T257.2.1.p: One wife shames a rival by exposing the second wife's bald head; the hair marvelously regrows.

T257.2.2.p: A jealous wife or mistress turns her rival into a hound (dog).

T257.3.p: A jealous husband is not punished because he is already suffering enough from his jealousy.

T257.4.r: I am a terrible sinner.” Mensa Philosophica No. 72; *Wesselski Mönchslatein No. 74. Cf. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
T257.4.p: A husband jealous of his wife's confession is punished by the priest; when he sees the priest take her behind the altar to punish her, he offers to take the punishment instead, and the wife tells the priest to beat him well.

T257.5.p: A jealous husband kills a nightingale because his wife gets up at night to listen to it.

T257.5.1.p: A woman's scented hair attracts deer, and her husband becomes jealous of them.

T257.6.p: A jealous king has handsome young captives massacred so that none can rival him.

T257.7.p: A husband's unjust jealousy drives his wife to actually commit adultery.

T257.7.1.p: A wife, wrongly accused of adultery by her husband, repays him by actually doing the same.

T257.8.p: A jealous husband is displeased that his wife enjoys sexual intercourse, believing she must have had previous lovers.

T257.9.p: A jealous husband spends all his earnings as a skilled smith paying courtiers to keep quiet about his wife, and finally locks her away in a hut in the forest.

T257.10.p: A trickster sends a jealous wife after her husband so that she is distracted and he can steal food.

T257.11.p: A jealous wife ties her husband to her so he cannot slip away to meet another woman.

T258.p: A wife who cannot resist finding out what is going on, prying into matters that do not concern her.

T258.1.r: She says, “Wait and see.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 242 No. 538.
T258.1.p: A curious wife tells her husband to wait and see what happens when they overhear thieves plotting to rob the house, kill him, and assault her. The husband wants to raise the alarm instead.

T258.1.1.p: A husband insists on learning a secret his wife is keeping, despite her reluctance to tell him.

T258.2.p: A wife insists on learning a secret her husband is keeping, despite his reluctance to tell her.

T261.p: A wife who repays her husband's kindness with betrayal or disloyalty.

T261.1.r: She is ungrateful. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 31.
T261.1.p: A husband takes his wife's place and is punished for her adultery.

T263.p: A wife who boasts of what she has done for her husband while never mentioning what she has done for herself.

T265.p: A woman shows her children to others as her treasures, calling them her jewels, instead of showing her personal jewelry.

T268.p: A beautiful woman is married to an ugly man; he is grateful for her, and she puts up with him patiently. She says that they have both gained paradise by this.

T271.p: A wife who is ignored or neglected by her husband.

T271.1.p: A woman gets rid of her impotent husband and remarries.

T271.1.1.p: The mistress of an impotent husband sends her maid out to find a man for her.

T272.p: A wife who refuses to speak.

T272.1.p: A silent wife is finally made to speak when her husband is in danger.

T274.p: A wife who cannot keep a secret and tells what she has been told.

T275.p: A wife who spends money recklessly and wastefully.

T280.p: Miscellaneous tales about other aspects of married life that do not fit the more specific headings.

T281.r: *Encyc. Religion Ethics s.v. “Adultery”; Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 149, *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 488; English: Wells 60 (Syre Gowene and the Carle of Carelyle); Icelandic: *Boberg.
T281.p: A host offers his wife, or his daughter, to a guest as a bed companion for the night.

T281.1.p: A host offers a bed companion, such as his wife or daughter, to a druid who is his guest.

T281.2.p: A host offers a bed companion, such as his wife or daughter, to a king or prince who is his guest.

T282.p: A barren wife gives her husband her handmaid as a wife, so that the handmaid can bear him children.

T282.1.p: A barren first wife insists that her husband take a second wife, who may bear him children.

T283.p: A wife refuses to sleep with her husband until he meets her demand.

T284.r: Chauvin II 97 No. 52; Panchatantra III 9 (tr. Ryder 341); Bødker Exempler 295 No. 57; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
T284.p: A frightened wife shows affection toward her husband, which is so unusual that he pardons the robber who frightened her.

T285.r: *Ward II 621 No. 30; Herbert III 18; *Crane Vitry 223 No. 223; Wesselski Mönchslatein 190 No. 149; Scala Celi 115a No. 639.
T285.p: A mistress who has always said her prayers is refused help by the Virgin Mary when she tries to win a husband from his wife, and the wife later tells the mistress, who repents.

T286.p: When the husband sees his mistress's ring, he stops having intercourse with his wife.

T287.r: N. A. Indian (Kaska): Teit JAFL XXX 457.
T287.p: A tale explaining why it is good for a virtuous woman to be separated from a wicked man.

T288.p: A wife refuses to sleep with a husband she dislikes.

T288.1.p: A wife whom the husband does not love curses him when he tries to force her to sleep with him.

T291.r: (1) Only her property is wanted; (2) her husband is still in her heart; (3) if new husband is bad it will not be well, if he is good there will be the fear that he will die. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 222.
T291.p: A tale explaining why a widow does not marry again.

T291.1.p: A wife vows never to marry again after her husband dies, and keeps the vow.

T292.p: A husband sells his wife against her will.

T292.1.p: Men exchange or trade their wives with one another.

T294.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Siberian and N. A. Indian: Jochelson JE VI 366.
T294.p: The husband or wife of a supernatural being longs for their old home and goes back to visit relatives.

T295.p: A husband boasts too freely about his wife's beauty, and this leads to his death: a friend secretly views the wife naked, and the wife, having learned of it, joins the man and together they kill the king.

T296.p: A wife buys, or sells, the right to spend one night with her husband.

T298.p: A couple who have separated come back together and are reconciled.

T299.p: A general heading for miscellaneous details of married life that do not fit elsewhere in the index.

T299.1.p: A husband falls asleep with his head resting in his wife's lap, showing affection between them.

T299.2.p: A wife gives her husband sensible advice or a careful warning.

T299.2.1.p: A wife warns her husband not to step on a piece of red cloth.

T299.2.2.p: A wife warns her husband, who is setting off on a journey or quest, to resist the seductions of other women.

T300.r: *Penzer III 172 n. 2; *Encyc. Religion Ethics III 474 s.v. “Chastity”; **J. Main Religious Chastity (New York, 1913); *E. Fehrle Die kultische Keuschheit im Altertum (Giessen, 1910).— Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman.
T300.p: A general heading for stories about staying sexually pure or abstaining from sex entirely.

T301.p: A person gives up their virginity as a sacrifice, often for a religious or higher purpose.

T302.p: The ways in which ascetics, or holy people who live in severe self-denial, practice their discipline.

T310.r: *Encyc. Religion Ethics III 271ff. s.v. “Celibacy”; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 163, 166, 261, (Greenland): Rink 410, Rasmussen I 137, 363, III 85, 154, 200, (Central): Boas RBAE VI 583, 637, (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 49.
T310.p: A general heading for stories in which people choose to remain unmarried or to abstain from sex.

T310.1.r: *Frazer Fasti IV 206ff.; **E. Fehrle Die kultische Keuschheit im Altertum (Giessen, 1910).
T310.1.p: Sexual relations are restricted to set times as part of a religious or ritual observance.

T310.1.1.p: Friday night, the eve of the Sabbath, is set aside only for marital intimacy.

T311.p: A woman does not want to marry and tries to avoid it.

T311.0.1.p: A woman's dislike of marriage begins after a dream that turns her against it.

T311.1.r: Type 888*; cf. Type 510B; *Toldo II 306; Alphabet No. 310; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Aeschylus Suppliants line 5; India: Thompson-Balys.
T311.1.p: A maiden, or a bridegroom, runs away to avoid the wedding.

T311.2.p: A woman chooses to stay chaste rather than remain married to a husband who cannot have sex.

T311.2.1.p: A girl kills herself rather than marry a man she does not love.

T311.3.p: A girl stays a virgin after both of her suitors are killed in battle.

T311.4.p: A warrior queen refuses to marry and fights her suitors, but is eventually defeated and married.

T312.p: The daughter of a saint dies when someone tries to court or seduce her.

T312.1.p: A woman dies when she loses her sanctity or purity.

T313.p: A girl who has been raped or ravished has her virginity miraculously restored by the Virgin Mary.

T313.1.p: A girl who has been raped or ravished has her virginity miraculously restored by a saint.

T313.1.1.p: A nun who is pregnant is made a virgin again through the power of a saint.

T314.p: A father kills his own daughter so that she will not become a prostitute.

T314.1.p: A father kills his daughter so that she will not become the property of a tyrant.

T315.p: A married couple remains chaste and abstains from sexual relations within marriage.

T315.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 689; Chaucer Second Nun’s Tale (St. Cecelia); *Toldo II 304ff.; Jewish: *Neuman, Gaster Exempla 200 No. 73.
T315.1.p: A married couple agrees together to abstain from sexual relations.

T315.2.p: A husband who practices sexual restraint and does not touch his wife, even though she desires him.

T315.2.1.p: A woman with a restrained husband or lover splashes water on her thighs as she crosses a stream, then scolds the water for being bolder than her husband, thereby drawing attention to her own situation.

T315.2.2.p: A wife scolds or shames her restrained husband by showing him the behavior of a cock and hens.

T315.2.2.1.p: A wife reforms her restrained husband by having the walls of the bedroom painted with erotic scenes.

T315.3.p: A woman remains continent through two marriages and then becomes a nun.

T317.p: A person overcomes sexual desire or lust by various means of self-discipline.

T317.1.p: A person suppresses lust by sitting in water.

T317.2.p: A person suppresses lust through prayer.

T317.3.p: A person suppresses lust through preaching.

T317.4.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 99; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
T317.4.p: A person suppresses lust through fasting.

T317.5.p: A man and a woman love each other chastely, without physical intimacy, for twenty-five years.

T317.6.p: A monk finds that only abuse and cruel treatment from his fellow monks can cure his lust.

T318.p: A wife proves her faithfulness, for example by standing in for her husband's mistress and later showing that her child is legitimate through tokens and a missing toe matching the husband's four-toed foot.

T320.r: Heptameron No. 26; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Schlauch Romance in Iceland (New York, 1934) 105f., *Boberg.
T320.p: A woman or girl escapes a lover or suitor she does not want, often by clever or forceful means.

T320.1.r: *Types 881, 882, 883AB, 888, 892; *Loomis White Magic 95; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
T320.1.p: A innocent woman repeatedly resists many attempts at seduction and escapes every one of them, keeping her faithfulness intact.

T320.1.1.p: A woman keeps her virginity even under torture, and the suitors who tried to win her finally give up their attempts.

T320.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
T320.2.p: A girl kills a man who threatens to violate her chastity.

T320.2.1.p: A woman who is escaping slavery kills a man who tries to rape her.

T320.3.p: A bride frightens off a man who tries to rape her.

T320.3.1.p: A widow puts on her late husband's armor and so frightens away a man who wants to ravish her.

T320.4.p: A wife escapes a king's lust by shaming him, causing him to give up his desire for her.

T320.4.1.p: A woman escapes a king's lust by making him smell her breath so badly that he loses interest.

T320.5.p: A girl gives up her wealth and flees to escape a lustful emperor.

T320.6.p: A wife sets fire to her own house to escape an undesired lover.

T321.p: A woman escapes an undesired lover through a miracle or divine intervention rather than her own action.

T321.1.p: A maiden who has vowed to remain celibate is given a beard in answer to her prayer, so that she is no longer desirable.

T321.2.r: *Ward II 628 No. 16, 697 No. 9; Scala Celi 115a No. 641; Von der Hagen III 451.
T321.2.p: A girl named Mary, bought by a knight, keeps her virginity because the Virgin appears to her.

T321.3.p: A knight spares a girl's virginity when he sees her surrounded by the Virgin and her attendants, after she has prayed for help.

T321.4.p: A girl prays to the Virgin to keep her virginity; two soldiers quarrel over possessing her, and their captain kills her, which is considered saving her.

T321.5.p: A sudden magical sickness or discomfort stops a lover from raping a woman.

T321.6.p: In answer to a maiden's prayer, a saint turns a boat off course and guides it to another place, saving her from a threat.

T322.p: A girl strikes a man who tries to kiss her, driving him off.

T322.1.p: A woman kicks a lecherous monk down the stairs to get rid of his advances.

T322.2.p: A princess threatens to kill a king who is pursuing her with unwanted love, and so frightens him off.

T322.3.p: A man who is pressing unwanted love on a girl is drugged and secretly carried out of her presence.

T322.4.p: A girl repels a lover by declaring that she has vowed to remain chaste.

T323.p: A woman escapes an unwanted lover through some clever stratagem or trick.

T323.1.p: A princess flees an unwanted lover by escaping in disguise as a bishop.

T323.2.p: A princess avoids an unwelcome lover by putting on a skin-coat that smells foul, so he will not want her.

T324.p: A girl keeps her virginity because an emissary treats her kindly and makes the lord think she is a relative, so he does not molest her.

T325.p: A chaste woman refuses the sexual advances of a conqueror who has taken her land or city.

T325.1.r: Has him try it on her. Cuts her head off. *Bonner Byzantion XIV 142ff.
T325.1.p: A chaste woman tricks a conqueror who wants her by promising him a drug that will make him invulnerable.

T326.p: A woman kills herself rather than lose her virginity.

T326.1.p: Girls drown themselves to keep their virginity.

T326.2.p: A man is killed while defending his sweetheart's honor, and she then kills herself.

T326.3.r: Der Heiligen Leben und Leiden 100ff. (Santa Barbara).
T326.3.p: A woman is put to death, as a martyr, rather than give up her virginity.

T327.r: (Cf. S160, T333.) Heptameron No. 10; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
T327.p: A woman maims her own body so that a lover will no longer desire her.

T327.1.r: Type 706; **Williamson Philological Quarterly XI 149; *BP I 303; *Crane Vitry 158 No. 57; Herbert III 72, 611; Hervieux IV No. 120; *Penzer III 20f.; Alphabet No. 136; *bin Gorion Born Judas@2 IV 175, 283; Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 11, 12; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 40; Nouvelles de Sens No. 12.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 2; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 273 n. 6; Africa (Bangola): Weeks 122.
T327.1.p: A maiden sends her lecherous lover, who is also her brother, her eyes, hands, or breasts, the body parts he had admired.

T327.2.p: A woman prays successfully for a disease to make herself repellent to a lover.

T327.3.p: A saint plucks out her own eye when pressed to marry, so that she becomes unattractive.

T327.4.p: Maidens smear themselves with blood to escape rape, making themselves appear unattractive or unclean.

T327.5.p: A woman raises sores on her body so that she will be unattractive and keep her chastity.

T327.6.p: A princess takes on a loathsome disguise to avoid a demon lover she does not want.

T327.7.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 871*; Russian: Andrejev No. 871*.
T327.7.p: A girl escapes an unwanted lover by cutting off her braids, so that she is no longer attractive to him.

T328.p: A girl lives in a tomb or burial vault to keep her chastity and avoid men.

T330.r: *Toldo II 304ff.; *Loomis White Magic 187 n. 140; Italian Novella: Rotunda.

T585.6.p: A newborn baby kisses its mother, who is dying.

T585.7.p: A precocious hero, while still a baby, climbs out of his cradle and sets off to fight in a war.

T585.8.r: Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 789, II 299.
T585.8.p: A child stands up or walks as soon as it is born.

T585.9.p: A child is born already circumcised.

T586.r: Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 85, 251.
T586.p: A woman gives birth to more than one child at once.

T586.1.r: BP I 432; Köhler-Bolte I 467; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 420; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 200f.; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 310 n. 116a; S. A. Indian (Chibcha): Alexander Lat. Am. 199.
T586.1.p: A woman gives birth to a large number of children at one time.

T586.1.1.p: A woman gives birth to four children at one time.

T586.1.1.1.p: A woman gives birth to six children at one time.

T586.1.2.r: *Fb “gifte” I 432; *BP I 432; Wesselski Märchen 174 No. 64; *Loomis White Magic 87; India: Thompson-Balys.
T586.1.2.p: A woman gives birth to seven children at one time.

T586.1.2.1.p: A king and queen have seven sons born together, and all are named Maine.

T586.1.2.2.p: A king has six or seven sons born together, and all are named Lugaid.

T586.1.3.p: A woman gives birth to nine children at one time.

T586.1.4.p: A woman gives birth to five children at one time in each of four successive years.

T586.1.5.p: Forty sons are born to one mother within a single day.

T586.2.p: A family has an unusually large number of children.

T586.2.1.p: A king has fifty sons (or daughters).

T586.2.2.p: A king has sixty thousand sons.

T586.3.r: (Cf. T587.1.) Irish myth: Cross; S. A. Indian (Tenetehara): Wagley-Galvao BBAE CXLIII (3) 148, (Kaigua, Tembé, Apapocuvá-guarani): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 136.
T586.3.p: A woman gives birth to several children at once because she had sexual relations with several men.

T586.3.1.p: Three brothers ravish a woman, and she then gives birth to triplets.

T586.3.2.p: Triplets are killed by their tribe as soon as they are born.

T586.4.p: An animal gives birth to an unusually large number of young at one time.

T586.4.1.p: A cow gives birth to four calves at one time.

T586.5.p: A woman gives birth again and again in unusually quick succession.

T586.5.1.p: A woman gives birth to a child every month.

T586.5.2.p: A child is born each day for seven days in a row.

T587.p: A woman gives birth to two babies at once.

T587.1.r: (Cf. T586.3.) *Harris Cult of the Heavenly Twins 10ff.; Krappe “Tyndare” Studi e Materiali di Storia delle Religioni XV (1939) 23—29; English: Child II 67 n., 511a, Wells 96 (Chevalere Assigne), 126 (Lai Le Freine), *Hibbard 295; Greek: Fox 79; India: Thompson-Balys.
T587.1.p: The birth of twins is taken as a sign that the wife has been unfaithful to her husband.

T587.2.p: Twins are born, one holding the other's ear in its mouth.

T587.2.1.p: Right after twins are born, one puts the other in his mouth, and that twin's body becomes made of iron.

T587.3.p: Of twins, the one born last is the one who was conceived first.

T588.p: Beliefs and customs connected with the afterbirth (placenta) that is expelled after a child is born.

T588.1.p: Spirits create a child out of the placenta.

T589.p: Miscellaneous motifs about childbirth that do not fit the other groups.

T589.1.p: Two wives each give birth to half a boy; when the halves are placed together they form a whole, living boy.

T589.2.r: N. A. Indian (Shoshonean): Alexander N. Am. 133, (California): Gayton and Newman 92.
T589.2.p: A boy is cut in two, and each half becomes a complete boy.

T589.3.r: (Cf. T589.7.1.) Type 303; Köhler-Bolte I 179; Fb “træ” III 865b; *Kittredge Arthur 171 n. 1; Irish myth: Cross.
T589.3.p: Trees appear at the moment a hero is born, and they serve as life tokens that show the hero's fortunes.

T589.4.p: A child born with a veil (a membrane over the face) brings its owner good luck.

T589.5.r: Fb “sjæl” III 214a; N. A. Indian: *Alexander N. Am. 281 n. 20.
T589.5.p: A newborn child is believed to be the rebirth of a person who has recently died. The child is thought to carry the dead person's soul or identity.

T589.6.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. IV 1342ff.; v. Wlislocki Germania N. R. XXII 134ff.
T589.6.p: Explanations adults give children about where babies come from. These are fanciful stories told in place of the facts of birth.

T589.6.1.p: A story that babies are brought by a stork. Adults tell children this as an explanation of birth.

T589.6.1.1.p: A vulture drops a newborn boy into the lap of a queen who is bathing, and she takes the child as her own.

T589.6.2.p: A story that babies are brought by a midwife. Adults tell children this as an explanation of birth.

T589.6.3.p: A story that children come from the underworld, the realm of the dead below the earth.

T589.6.4.p: A story that children come out of a well. Adults tell children this as an explanation of birth.

T589.6.5.p: A story that children grow on or come from cauliflower plants. Adults tell children this as an explanation of birth.

T589.6.6.p: A story that children come from stones. Adults tell children this as an explanation of birth.

T589.7.p: Two births happen at the same moment, such as a child and an animal, or a hero born at a notable time.

T589.7.1.p: A domestic animal and a human child are born at the same moment.

T589.7.2.p: A hero is born during the same hour as Christ's Nativity, the birth of Jesus.

T589.8.p: A woman tries to hold off giving birth so that the child will be born on a lucky, favorable day.

T589.9.p: A child has several mothers, for example a birth mother and one or more others who raise or claim the child.

T590.p: A general heading for miscellaneous motifs about conception and birth that do not fit the more specific groups.

T591.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 113, 441 n. 78; *Boje 107; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T591.p: A person becomes unable to conceive children, or a man becomes impotent, because of magic cast by someone.

T591.1.r: (Cf. D1347, D1925, D2161.3.11.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
T591.1.p: Magical cures or remedies used to overcome barrenness or impotence caused by magic.

T591.1.1.p: A magic potion is given to a man to cure his impotence.

T591.1.2.p: A man drinks the milk of a hornless cow of a single color so that his wife will become pregnant.

T591.2.p: It is bad luck for a woman to look at the face of a childless person, since this may make her unable to have children.

T592.p: A woman who has no milk suddenly has milk flowing in her breasts, often as a sign or miracle.

T592.1.p: A medicine or potion causes a woman's breasts to fill with milk.

T595.r: *Type 451; BP I 70ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 8.
T595.p: A sign is hung out to tell waiting brothers whether the mother has given birth to a boy or a girl.

T596.p: Children are given their names, often in a notable or miraculous way.

T596.1.p: An angel gives a child its name.

T596.2.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 521a; Irish myth: Cross.
T596.2.p: Children are given names that are simply numbers, such as One, Two, Three.

T597.p: A father's ambitions or wishes are passed on to his child at the moment of conception.

T600.r: **Ploss Das Kind; Fellinger Das Kind in der altfranzösischen Literatur (Göttingen, 1908); *McDaniel Conception, Birth and Infancy (Miami, 1948); Irish myth: *Cross.
T600.p: General heading for stories and motifs about looking after children.

T601.p: A baby is bathed in milk.

T602.p: Weapons and horses are obtained for a boy at his birth, so he is equipped for life or adventure.

T605.p: A god or divine being serves as a child's nurse.

T610.p: General heading for stories and motifs about how children are nourished and grow up.

T611.p: A child is fed by sucking at a breast or other source of nourishment.

T611.1.p: A child survives by sucking on its own fingers instead of being fed by anyone else.

T611.1.1.r: Egyptian: Müller 115; India: Thompson-Balys; Hindu: Keith 166.
T611.1.1.p: A child is nourished by sucking the thumb of a god.

T611.2.p: A father miraculously nurses his child at his own breast.

T611.3.r: Hoffman-Krayer Zs. f. Vksk. XXV 121 n. 4; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3297, Legends No. 528.
T611.3.p: A witch or fairy nurses a child.

T611.4.p: Children are magically prevented from nursing or being suckled.

T611.5.p: A saint miraculously nurses a child.

T611.5.1.p: A saint has two breasts, one giving milk and one giving honey, and uses them to nurse two infants.

T611.5.2.p: A saint feeds a child by cutting off a cow's teats and pouring milk into the child's mouth from them.

T611.5.3.p: An angel miraculously nurses children so they survive without a human mother.

T611.6.r: (Cf. T592.) Loomis White Magic 22; India: Thompson-Balys.
T611.6.p: A woman's breast miraculously produces milk so she can nurse an orphan child.

T611.7.p: A child abandoned in the wild is kept alive by seagulls, nursed with milk from a doe, and given a bell by an angel to drink from.

T611.8.p: A single woman nurses many babies at once.

T611.9.p: A dead mother's breasts keep providing enough milk to feed her baby for two years.

T611.10.p: A man is suckled by a dog or wolf as a child and is named Mac Con, meaning Son of Dog.

T611.10.1.p: A girl raised by a wolf has a claw-like fingernail resembling a wolf's nail.

T611.10.2.p: A saint is nursed by a wolf as a baby.

T611.11.p: A child survives by sucking the eyeballs of a snake or frog mother who has abandoned it.

T612.r: Oceanic: Dixon 132, 137; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 319 n. 152.
T612.p: A child born after its mother has been killed takes care of itself during infancy without any adult help.

T615.3.p: A child is unusually wise from a very young age.

T615.4.p: A clever young boy supports himself and his widowed mother through his cunning and wits.

T615.5.p: A very young child, unusually precocious, asks for weapons.

T617.r: English: Wells 72 (Sir Percyvelle of Galles); Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman.
T617.p: A boy is raised without knowing anything of the outside world.

T617.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 69.
T617.1.p: A future hero, kept apart from the world as a child, kills ever larger game with better and better weapons.

T617.2.p: A hero first learns his own name when he sets out on his first adventure.

T621.r: (Cf. L111.4.1.) N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 69.
T621.p: An orphan asks about his parents, wanting to learn who they were and what became of them.

T640.p: Children born outside marriage, and the matters of their upbringing and status.

T640.1.p: The child of a nun is born out of wedlock and is a central element of the story.

T640.2.p: The mother of an illegitimate child is handed over as a pledge or guarantee for a crime committed by the child.

T642.p: A test of whether children are legitimate: they are exposed to asps (venomous snakes), which will bite only foreigners and spare true-born children.

T644.p: A child reveals, through his own words or deeds, that he is illegitimate.

T645.r: *Type 873; *Potter Sohrab and Rustem 6ff.; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 86, 330, 478f.
T645.p: A lover leaves a token with the girl he has been with so that she can give it to their son when he grows up.

T645.1.p: A man leaves a sword for his posthumous son, who is to use it to kill the man who murdered his father.

T645.2.p: A hero leaving a girl tells her what to do depending on the sex of the child she may bear: keep a daughter, send a son to him.

T645.2.1.p: A hero leaving a girl tells her to kill the baby if it turns out to be a daughter.

T645.3.p: A father orders the mother to send the expected illegitimate son to him once the boy can perform certain feats.

T645.4.p: A hero leaves his bedmate the keys to a treasure chamber, meant for the son she is expected to bear.

T647.p: A law or rule makes it illegal to take care of an illegitimate child.

T670.p: A child is taken in and raised as the adopted child of another person or couple.

T671.p: An ogress suckles a hero and then claims him as her own son, so that he is adopted through nursing.

T672.p: An adopted child rebukes his foster mother and is sent back to his real mother.

T673.p: A rich but stingy couple adopt a young man as their son, and everyone ends up happy.

T674.p: An adopted child is abandoned after the couple have a child of their own.

T675.p: A child abandoned by his mother suckles from the whole flock of goats or sheep but is still not satisfied, and only his real mother will do.

T675.1.p: A child prefers its foster mother to its real mother.

T676.p: A childless couple adopt an animal to raise as if it were their child.

T676.1.r: (Cf. D191.) Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 5.
T676.1.p: A childless woman adopts a snake that is really a man transformed into a serpent.

T677.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 701*; Russian: Andrejev No. 703.
T677.p: An elderly childless couple make a child substitute out of wood, snow, clay or similar material.

T678.p: An adopted child looks exactly like the real child raised alongside him.

T680.p: A general heading for miscellaneous tales about the care and raising of children.

T681.1.p: Other animals mock an owl for being proud of his son's ugly feet, which they consider hideous.

T682.p: A hero is born after his father has died.

T684.p: The devil takes the place of a newborn baby, substituting himself for the child.

T685.p: A general heading for stories about twins.

T685.1.p: Twins go out together on adventures.

T685.2.r: *Dickson 98ff.; *Krappe Balor 30, 143 n. 33, FL XXXIV 189ff.; Gaster Oldest Stories 168.
T685.2.p: Twins are hostile to each other.

T685.3.p: Twins look exactly alike, so they are hard to tell apart.

T685.4.p: Of twins, the one born first grows steadily weaker while the one born second grows stronger as they are raised.

T686.p: Four children born at once become heroes.

T687.p: Three children born at once become heroes.
